speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacLean (Minister of Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
subtopic: ALTERATION OF LOBSTER SEASON IN CERTAIN DISTRICTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, due to the very difficult climatic conditions recently experienced in many parts of the maritime provinces, it is now fairly obvious that lobster fishermen would have great difficulty in commencing their season's operations in districts 7-A and 7-B on the normal opening date of May 1. These districts cover, in the main, the northeastern coast of New Brunswick, the outer coast of Prince Edward Island, the strait of Canso, part of Northumberland strait and the west coast of Cape Breton.
Officials of my department have been watching the situation carefully. We have also received a large number of representations from the fishermen for consideration in these rather unique conditions. For these reasons I am proposing to postpone the opening date of the season in districts 7-A and 7-B from May 1 to May 10, and the closing date from June 30 to July 5. It is my hope that this action and the expected return to normal weather will enable the fishermen to prosecute a full fishery with no more difficulty than is usually experienced.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
As I said a moment ago, at this approximate period of the session it is customary for a motion to be made extending the hours of sitting of the house. As I look back prior to the time we assumed office, such motions were made in several years on the 69th, the 71st, the 78th, the 84th and the 88th days.

Business oj the House
I believe it is in the interests of all hon. members to endeavour at all times to proceed expeditiously with the business of the house. The extension of hours which is being sought will, I feel, be beneficial. It will bring about an actual addition of approximately 18 extra days between now and the first day of July. I mention that particular date not because there is any special significance to it with reference to parliament and the continuation of the session, but simply to show that the extra hours will mean that considerable additional time will be made available to deal with the various matters of legislation which remain to be considered this session.
Of course, in giving to the house a general outline of the legislative program I know there will be a full realization of the fact that the list in question is not an all-inclusive one, and that it does not include matters which conceivably could arise during the balance of the session. There might be some who would feel that the added hours place an extraordinarily heavy responsibility on members of parliament. I again remind hon. members that the hours of sitting in this house are far less, in the very beginning of the session, than is the case in the mother of parliaments. So far, up until April 21, we had been in session for 88 days, and it is of interest to ascertain the division in the calendar of the various matters that have come before the house.
The speech from the throne, including the opening day, took three days. The debate on what is called the baby budget took six days; private members' Mondays, six days; private members' Thursdays, two days; three supply motions, six days; the debate on March 3 on a matter of urgent public importance, one day. That is a total of 24 days in respect of debates that are fixed by the rules and the special debate. Then in supply on the supplementary estimates, four days; interim supply, two days. The main estimates, which to date have comprised the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, the Department of Agriculture and the Post Office Department, all of which have been completed, and the Departments of Labour and Northern Affairs and National Resources, incomplete, have taken 17 days, making a total for supply of 23 days, which incidentally, I believe, is somewhat longer than the total period taken in respect of supply in other parliaments.
When I mention the mother of parliaments I am not in any way suggesting that this house should follow the course followed there, but mention it simply by way of explanation that, in the experience of the years, the British parliament, which has been generally

a model of expedition, has found it unnecessary to go into detail item by item in the estimates. I think the general plan there is for members to pick out particular items. All of us know, and I have that knowledge from having been in the opposition, that when each item is called, it is surprising the impetus and encouragement the calling of the items has to bring to the attention of the house matters which otherwise might not have been referred to. They are matters of much interest but not always of the same relative importance. On legislation so far we have spent 41 days, and have completed 17 bills and two motions.
I undertook to give a general outline, and naturally the house would like to have some idea as to the legislation projected or anticipated and yet to be introduced. In addition to the items in routine proceedings there will be amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act; an amendment to the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act; amendments to the Criminal Code, including capital punishment; an amendment to the narcotics control legislation; an amendment to the Coal Production Assistance Act; amendment to the Financial Administration Act; ratification of the convention on the law of the sea, the Pine Point Railway Act and the Food and Drugs Act amendments.
In addition, legislation will probably be introduced with respect to amendments to the Loan Companies Act, the Industrial Development Bank Act, the assignment of crown debts legislation and the War Veterans' Allowance Act. There will, of course, be a budget debate and legislation will be based on the resolutions. Furthermore, considerable attention will have to be given to the transportation problem and legislation arising out of, if not directly founded on, certain portions of the report of the royal commission on transportation may be anticipated. In this connection there is one piece of legislation having to do with the act to make provision for the reduction of certain class and commodity rates on freight traffic or, as cited, the Freight Rates Reduction Act of 1959, which was extended in 1960. Application will be made to the house for approval of further extension of this act.
What I have said I think gives some indication of the considerable amount of legislation that yet remains for the attention of the house. As I said earlier, in the normal course of events there will, of course, be one or more matters which have not yet come before the cabinet but which no doubt will come before it between now and the conclusion of the session.

I take it that the government has been driven to put this motion on the order paper now for two reasons; first, because of the fact that the session began in November of last year, earlier than usual; and second, because of the long list of legislation announced by the Prime Minister, which is indicative of the tremendous amount of work still to be done. The fact is that most of the time has been taken up by government speakers. I said I would give some indication of this situation and I should now like to do so.
I have before me a list of the time taken by speakers for the different parties in a number of debates. This list was prepared
Business of the House
at my request by the whip's office and I have every reason to believe it is accurate. I bring to the attention of the house the fact that on many occasions speakers from the government side have risen to compliment the minister concerned, to thank him for the resolution introduced and to tell him what a tremendous benefit it was going to be in the riding of the member speaking, and I ask the house whether repetition of that same sort of thing day in and day out could not be eliminated and a great deal of the time of the house saved thereby.

Then there was Bill No. C-49 with regard to technical training assistance, which was discussed on December 7 and 9 and on which 13 government speakers took up 3 hours and 1 minute, we

in the opposition took up 1 hour and 16 minutes and the C.C.F. took up 32 minutes. The same thing can be said of the productivity council resolution, where 43 minutes were taken up by all the government speakers as compared with 15 minutes for this side of the house and 10 minutes for the C.C.F. I	could go on, because I have a complete list; however, that is indicative of the attitude and the statement I made a moment ago, namely that we on this side of the house are not those who are taking up the time in dealing with these matters.
The government evidently believe that the solution for this state of affairs is to provide more time for talk. That is a very inadequate objective unless the time so provided is profitably used by a clear cut division and organization of the work of the house. The fact that the members of the House of Commons have been talking since November 17 and that such little progress has been made is clear proof that something better is required in the way of planning the business of this house. But in this motion the government obviously believe that the best solution is to provide more time for more talk.
This particular motion, if accepted, will add
II	hours to the weekly sittings of the house except during the weeks when there are supply motions, when there are added 5 additional hours. Here, as I say, we are asked to extend the hours of the sitting of the house in order to deal with government business. However, when it comes to dealing with a supply motion, something which is the prerogative of the opposition, we are not allowed to sit longer so far as that is concerned. In any event, the object of this motion is to provide the equivalent of two full days of sitting per week. speakerposition: Prime Minister

speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
If the Prime Minister will allow me to complete my remarks I think he will find the answer to the question he has just asked. I was going on to say that I understood it to be the intention of the

government to conclude the sittings of this house by the end of June. This would give us a period of nine weeks within which to complete our work if we began morning sittings on Monday next. The equivalent of 15J days would be added to the work of the house within the next 9 weeks. The effect of this proposal is to reduce the length of the session by about three weeks. Without adding further hours at this stage, and on the assumption that the pace of work would remain the same regardless of hours of sitting, the session would probably expire on July 25 or thereabouts.
We find this proposal objectionable for two reasons. First, it provides for morning sittings at an unusually early period of the session; but what is more important, it comes at a time when the committees which normally meet in the morning are just getting down to work. In that respect here are the facts. There are 24 committees in existence or in contemplation. Of these, 14 have already started to work, 18 have been organized, and 11 have had sittings regularly. Over and above that, there are four special committees that have been appointed and three of these have had regular meetings. None the less there are five committees which have been organized but have not started to work, three of which in fact are extremely important.
Then the other objection we find is that there is no provision that the extra time provided will be used properly through better organization. I want to make a proposal to the government. Our proposal will make unnecessary morning sittings which at this stage prevent effective committee work, will provide for a different but more productive allocation of the time remaining, and will oblige the government to get busy in planning the remaining work of the session in the days that lie ahead.
Our proposal consists of three points. We propose first that we deal differently with the two remaining supply motions. The official opposition is willing to dispense with the debate on possibly both the remaining supnly motions. We would wish, however, to reserve our right to debate one of these motions for at least one day if circumstances call for such a debate. By making this proposal in connection with the supply motion we suggest that the government agree to call one such motion at the request of the opposition. That might not be necessary. If this first part of the proposal were put into effect, that would make available at once at least three days and possibly four days in which to deal with legislation and estimates.
The next point in the proposal is that the time spent on the budget debate-and I refer to the budget which the Minister of Finance

intends to bring down at a later date-be reduced from six days to four days. We think this proposal is justified because we have already spent six days in debating the supplementary budget, and because we feel that a four day budget debate, provided the evening sittings can be extended if members wish to speak, would ensure that all points of view would be heard. This proposal would make available an additional two days in which to deal with estimates and legislation.
We asked that the government make available the final and complete list of legislation which it intends to place before the house. The Prime Minister has now done this. We should like to study this list at once so that we could-if it is the wish of the government to co-operate with the various leaders of the house-develop a definite time schedule for each item of legislation and each department of the government. It seems to me that we could very easily, having regard for this list, set aside a certain number of hours or days for each item on the program which we could attempt to follow unless such an adherence in a particular case would not be in the public interest. For instance as I look at the list which I took down I find that there are a number of items which could be disposed of in no time. I could almost immediately give the assurance to the government that at least one of these measures, if I understand it correctly, should take little time at all.
On the other hand there are measures of extreme importance. Without mentioning them, I have one in mind wherein we might say, "We will set aside X number of days to deal with this legislation," and we will give the undertaking that beyond that we will not go; with this exception, that if it became clear to us during the course of the debate that more speakers were required, we would ask that the hours of sitting of that day be extended so we could dispose of that legislation in the allotted time.
If such a time schedule were arranged, I can see no objection to extending the evening sittings of the house beyond the present sitting hours, within the confines of any such schedule of days. I may add that we have no objection to sitting an additional hour in the evening, say from 7.30 until 10.30, as the motion indicates. This would be a gain of approximately five days which, when added to the two proposals we made previously, gives a total of 10 to 11 additional days. Add to that a better organization of the business of the house, as I indicated in my last point, and I think we will have gone a long way toward meeting the desire or wish of all hon. members, not only those of the government, for an orderly consideration of the business.
Business of the House
It seems to us that this additional time, combined with the suggestion for planning and organization which I have made, would allow us to complete our work within the period of time which I believe the government has in mind. I see no point, however, in adding more hours, providing for more talk, and more time, without better management and organization.
There is another objection which I bring to the attention of the government. It deserves to be considered. It is the fact that additional hours work a great hardship on the staff. I need not tell the Prime Minister this; I am sure he realizes it every bit as much as I. We know what happened during the extension of the hours last year, when two members of the Hansard staff were stricken rather seriously. This also affects the very active and dynamic group of young page boys who give us such devoted service. Because of the fact that the hours begin earlier it will not be possible for them to attend school, as they have in the past. Also, this is a very critical period of the year, namely examination time.
The Prime Minister spoke a moment ago about the mother of parliaments and what was being done in the parliament of the United Kingdom. I have before me the report dated February 19, 1959, from the select committee on procedure. An attempt was made to have morning sittings and the parliament of the United Kingdom decided against them. This can be found at pages 13 to 15. I will only read the pertinent sentence, and I quote from page 15 of the report from the select committee on procedure:
For this reason, and in view of the disadvantages which attach to morning sittings and in our view outweigh the possible advantages, we recommend no change in the present practice in regard to morning sittings.
It is true that in reply one can say there is a different arrangement in the United Kingdom. However, I am suggesting a different arrangement in the work and the planning of the business of this house.
I ask the government, therefore, in the light of what I have said and in the light of the proposal I have put forward, not to proceed with this motion today but to consider the proposals I have made in all seriousness and in all good faith in an attempt to assist the house and parliament to get on with the business. I am completely satisfied that a satisfactory arrangement could be worked out among the various house leaders which would do away with morning sittings, if not altogether, at least until the dying days of the session.

Business of the House

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister was the first to comment on the comparison of this house with the mother of parliaments, I wish he would also underline to the house that there are over 600 members in the British House of Commons, and over 500 of them live within three hours of Westminster. This makes quite a difference in their ability to attend when there are extended hours.
This particular motion affects each one of us as individuals and then there is the party sense of which we are all conscious. The house may remember that in the past three sessions, on the introduction of similar motions the C.C.F. party objected very stridently though notoriously to no avail, and the hours were lengthened.
This occasion brings us forward with a different, more co-operative attitude. This is not based on any view of the government as a villain trying to seduce us poor Nells over in the corner. There is almost complete unanimity that we should complete this session by the end of June if we possibly can. There is still much to do and there is still a certain sense of urgency both in the house and in the country that there are problems to be met. If we do not complete the session by the end of June or shortly thereafter, I think every one of us in the house must bear some burden of the blame, although the apportionment will always be a controversial matter. If the session drags and dowdies, is it primarily because of the lack of government leadership in the house, as has been indicated by the hon. member for Laurier, or is it primarily because of the obstreperous behaviour or prolixity of opposition speakers?
As an advocate of a "complex theory" of the House of Commons I would not want to give a firm answer to either of these questions. However, I would suggest that all the following facts or factors are involved. I think most of us assume that this is a national forum and that the nation is listening to us or watching us, although if we think about it I think we can all have very grave doubts as to whether this is really true.
The second point is that the majority of us, whatever our party or our individual status as politicians, recognize that time is wasted in this house in a number of ways; by overlong question periods, by repetitious speeches, by the sudden temper or whim of various ones among us, or by just misunderstandings over the course of business. Another point is that under regular hours, or extended hours, an extra burden to attend the house and committees is placed upon hon. members from distant places. This burden is increasingly noted whenever we get into extended hours.

Another point is that many hon. members of this house, despite the fact that we are all peers, or we are assumed to be peers one to the other, have much different attitudes towards attendance either in Ottawa or in the house. Many hon. members carry on businesses or law practices co-ordinate with their political duties. Many others find a greater role to play politically at home, in their constituencies, than they do in Ottawa, even during sessions. Some of us, by geographic incident, our age or lack of age, our trade or profession or lack of either, or the nature and attitude of our constituents, cannot be the political semi-pros that I have just referred to. Also, a goodly number of us find that for family and financial reasons, the longer the session lasts, the rougher and tougher is our economic predicament.
Overlying all these individual factors is the crucial one of uncertainty; uncertainty not only as to the length of the session and the dates of the session, but uncertainty even about the length of this particular parliament. There have been many suggestions for change or reform put forward by members of the house over the years, including proposals that we should split the sessions, fix the length of the sessions, confine the length of the debates, accept as a principle that being a member of parliament is a full-time vocation and arrange the parliamentary year in a regular pattern with regular duties as they have really reached the stage of doing in Britain. Another suggestion has been put forward that we should increase the role of the house committees and cut down on formal debates in the house, together with a much greater degree of inter-party negotiation, as suggested by the hon. member for Laurier, in order to speed proceedings and get them under way.
It seems to me that one can detect one major difference of opinion among members of this house-and this has nothing to do with party positions-and this difference seems to me to rest on the basis of whether they were elected for the first time before or after 1957. There is much more patience among the more veteran members regarding the length of sessions and the length of debates. Perhaps because of the influx of rather young members in 1957, and particularly in 1958, this newer group is much more ready to say "The devil take it. Let's get through the job; let's get out of here to our families and our constituencies."
Speaking as an individual and not as a party member it is apparent, I think, where I stand on this point of view. This dialectic between the patience of experience and the impatience of the newer members probably affects all parties in the house. In any event,

the sense of urgency we express at this time is that we should speed this session to a conclusion. We see little reason on the order paper, or from what the Prime Minister has said, to seriously consider why we should be here throughout July. The added hours will be a blight to every one of us and especially to all those who take their attendance and their duties here seriously, though I ask the whole house to remember that there are many members who do not take this attendance seriously.
We intend to co-operate especially for this reason-and we are selfish in this, because most of us do come from distant places- that we cannot be at home week ends even if we wish to; and in order to end more quickly the load-and we know this view is shared by many of our colleagues who come from the west or from distant places in the east-we wish to amend the motion which has been put forward. We take the view that the whole hog is as palatable as the greater part, and I move, seconded by the hon. member for Skeena:
That the motion be amended by adding thereto:
Saturday, 11.00 a.m. to 1.00 p.m.; 2.30 p.m. to 6.00 p.m.

-yet during those all important discussions sitting hours were allowed to extend until six o'clock in the morning. In the United Nations I feel problems cannot be resolved on matters of life and death, by brilliant people of all the nations, on such a basis.
So much for what took place last week. I feel the same way about proceedings in the House of Commons. I have said before, time after time over the past eight years, that we are the 265 directors of the business of Canada. We have been given the responsibility for imposing laws which must be obeyed by the 18 million people who live in this country. We make the law, or rescind the law; we impose taxation and spend the money. As a rule the major business comes at the latter part of the session, and I say we are betraying the 18 million and those who elected us if our work is carried on in such haste that, taking account of the work to be done outside of the house, the hours and duties are such that we cannot give proper consideration and proper attention to decisions which are going to affect every man, woman and child in this country.

When this matter was discussed in the fall of 1957, and a motion was made by the chairman of one of the committees for simultaneous sittings very early in the session, the Prime Minister said that he recognized the position of members of the opposition; he had sat in the opposition, he knew of the difficulties, and he wanted to give the assurance that he would see to it that the business of the house was so arranged that no member would be denied the opportunity of properly discharging his responsibilities as a member of this house.

that I wanted to give hon. members the opportunity to expedite the business of the house.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the views expressed by the hon. member for Laurier. He is an experienced member of the house. I think he is able to teach a lesson to the hon. member for Essex East as to the proprieties. He presented his case in a most reasonable manner and must thereby have shocked the sensibilities of the hon. member for Essex East. He presented a viewpoint that met with a good deal of support on my part as I listened to him. There is a need for the reformation of the rules of the house. At the present time a committee is sitting, as did the committee last year, endeavouring to bring about changes which will expedite the business but which will not deny the fullest and most complete discussion of those questions that arise in respect of which there is bound to be controversy.
It is as though something unusual had happened. The hon. member for Essex East said that this is a most unusual circumstance, referring to the introduction of this motion at the present time. While I have already pointed it out, if I must do so I will repeat it and give the fullest information in that connection. I looked over the record and I found that in 1947, on the 78th day of the session, the sittings were extended. Then in 1949 the session was divided. In the first session prior to its conclusion morning sittings began on the 38th day and in the second session following the conclusion of the 42nd day. In the regular session of 1950 the house opened on February 16 and morning sittings began on the 69th day which fell on June 1. In 1951 the house opened on January 30 and morning sittings began on June 11 which was the 88th day. In the second session of 1951 morning sessions began on the 45th day. In the session of 1952 morning sessions began on the 71st day. In the 1952-53 session morning sittings began on the 84th day. Both the 195253 session and the 1953-54 session began in the fall of the year and in the 1953-54 session morning sittings began on May 31. Again in 1955 the situation was similar. All through the record in every year, with I think two exceptions, the house has commenced morning sittings on from the 71st day to the 88th day. Those were the halcyon days when hon. gentlemen opposite occupied the treasury seats. They said that was the proper course to follow and that it was necessary to have morning sittings.
My suggestion was not accepted. A further amendment has been accepted whereby sittings will also take place on Saturdays. I can understand the reason for that. Members who

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
I emphasize this point. The opposition had many more hon. members than were necessary to rise and secure a division. They sat silent, excepting for three who stood. The hon. member for Essex East saw what was going on behind his back while he faced the opposition, a not unusual position for him to occupy or adopt. They sat and they waited, and they waited until the Speaker declared the amendment passed. Then they rose and raised strong objection.
As far as Saturday sittings are concerned, I think no harm will be done to the opposition and I would be the last to do anything that would prevent them talking. I say this, Mr. Speaker, because as I have gone across this country I have learned that the more they talk, the better for the government, if their

Business of the House
criticism is like some of their recent criticism in regard to measures beneficial to Canada which have been opposed simply for the sake of opposing them.
Let me go on from there. They pose today as lovers of parliament. I think Saturdays could well be set aside, if the house agrees, for dealing with the supply of various departments. There will be that fine spirit of co-operation of which hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken. On Saturdays various departments could be dealt with. I would not want to see controversial measures dealt with on Saturdays because I would want to be assured that as many hon. members as possible would be present, not only from the opposition but on the government side. In any event, I think we could get together when controversial matters are to be discussed.
I think a step forward has been made today in this regard. On Saturdays we could deal with supply in respect of which, by agreement among the leader of the government in the house, the hon. member for Laurier and the hon. member for Kootenay West, they would have no difficulty in getting together and reaching the fullest agreement. These matters could be discussed on Saturday without in any way depreciating the opportunity of the opposition, including the hon. member for Essex East-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext: You know that is not true.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
-to fully discuss matters as they arise.
I cannot let this opportunity pass. One hon. member opposite said he could not believe that my immediate predecessors would ever have allowed anything being done which would shock the parliamentary tradition. What has been done today has given the house every opportunity. The house took its stand on this amendment and it was passed on division. I again underline the fact that those who yell the loudest opposite were the most silent until they were sure that the amendment had in fact been passed. Then they rose.
They talk about those other days. I am not going to go back over those days. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate read an excerpt from a statement I had made regarding parliament. Mr. Speaker, do they forget the crimes they committed against parliament? Do they forget those days of 1955 and 1956? I am not going into particulars unless they ask for them. They muzzled parliament-

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext: Nothing like this government. This government is the greatest muzzier of all parliaments.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
I remember what they did to the rights of parliament. Do they remember that black Friday when they trampled on the rights of parliament? One of the leaders in that regard was the vocal hon. gentleman from Essex East.
I quote an article with approbation. I have before me-I sent for it while the hon. gentleman was speaking-the University of Waterloo Review. I know the hon. gentleman has read it. The article is entitled "The Fifties: An Ottawa Retrospect" and it is written by Mr. Michael Barkway.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext: A friend of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext: He is not generally a friend of this government, as he does not approve of what we do.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext: He is finding out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
However, he did have some views on those who sit opposite today, the three horsemen. Yes, they indeed belong to the Apocrypha. They trod on the rights of parliament and destroyed every principle for which parliament has stood through the years. And they rise today and say that because they failed to demand a vote on the amendment, which was accepted by them in silence, their rights were taken away.
We did not impose this amendment on the official opposition. The amendment was from the C.C.F., or the New Party, whichever the expression may be that applies at the moment. They sat silent. Never did the opposition place before the house an amendment that was generally acceptable until after it had been passed.
What does Mr. Barkway say? He is one observer who lived through this period in Ottawa, and he is speaking of the period between 1955 and June of 1957 as he refers to a book by James Eayrs:
But I am one observer who lived through the period in Ottawa and find the memory both poignant and painful. They were always foreboding: a Canadian Gotterdammerung, unrealized or misunderstood by its principal actors.
There is no question that the political gods were old and tired.
These are they who now speak of parliamentary greatness. Then Mr. Barkway continues:
By October, 1955, the cabinet was unhappy and rudderless.
The hon. gentleman speaks about the days of my predecessors. I am reading an article by a man who is not unfriendly to the opposition. Mr. Barkway goes on to say:
Its self-preoccupation largely detached it from public sentiment. It was giving first priority to the difficult task of hanging together. In June 1957, at the end of the period covered by Mr. APRIL 24, 1961
Eayrs' book, it accomplished the task in a manner which few of its ministers had thought conceivable; nine of them mounted a common gallows.
These are the words of a gentleman who, as I say, is not unfriendly to the opposition. Then he makes an observation regarding the hon. member for Essex East which I think is particularly appropriate today. This is why 1 sent out for this booklet. He describes the bungling, myopia and the self-preoccupation and smugness of the Liberals. He does not think much of us, either. Then he says;
Dr. Eayrs most properly devotes the longest chapter of his book to this subject. It is sandwiched between an account of the travails of the truce commissions in Indo-China and a spine-tingling tale of Mr. Paul Martin's efforts at the UN assembly of 1955 to secure the admission of new members (which loses nothing of excitement by drawing heavily on Mr. Martin's own version of it).

subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext: I must read that article.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: EXTENSION OF HOURS OF SITTING ON AND AFTER MAY 1
speechtext:
This is dealing with those days of alleged parliamentary greatness. Then the article goes on to say:
Examples of the confusion and mismanagement in this most vital area of foreign policy could fill a book.
Then he goes on to say-and I will deal with this in future days in the form of fair debate if the opportunity arises-
Astounding as this was, it was not the worst of it. The worst of it, which has never before been told is that the draft note-
This has to do with the Columbia.
-which Mr. Pearson and Mr. St. Laurent both approved did not mention the adequacy of the 1909 treaty; it actually said that it was not adequate to deal with the Columbia case.
Then follow the words:
There can seldom have been a more timorous or unnecessary surrender.
I have given just a brief outline. I know hon. members will be encouraged to read the rest about those who in their day and generation did their best to destroy parliament, intimidate the opposition, refuse to accept any suggestion if it did not come from those surrounding them. And they tell us today that we have done a hurt to parliament. I think we have gone further than any government has gone before in giving the house and the private members of parliament the right to determine one thing: how long do they want to sit? Is it fair that we should sit for but a few hours a day as has been the case in the past for a long period of time and then, in the end, deny the fullest discussion? By what we are doing we shall provide the opposition with the fullest opportunity to discuss the issues and to debate them. On Saturdays, if hon. gentlemen opposite desire, there is no reason whatever why we should
Business of the House
not by agreement be able to choose for discussion subjects that will not be controversial.
One word as to the observations of the hon. member for Laurier. The hon. gentleman is experienced. He has shown a sense of restraint and wide knowledge as he placed before the house his ideas. The hon. member for Port Arthur, taking a similar attitude, did the same and I feel that the suggestions made deserve to be studied. What we must try to do is to make parliament more effective and more efficient while at the same time denying to no member the fullest opportunity to discuss, to criticize and suggest alternatives, for unless there is that discussion there cannot be the attainment of any objective of legislation which is both beneficial and effective.
I will do everything I can on the basis of the recommendations made by those two hon. gentlemen. I place myself behind several of them most strongly and I hope the committee as it meets will be able to determine what changes should be recommended which will bring about the fullest discussion while maintaining at the same time a degree of responsibility in carrying out the trust which has been placed with us. In all the circumstances, of course, in so far as the motion is concerned, in view of the unanimity which has been expressed, with the exception of three who stand alone, I feel we should accept the amendment to the motion, and then in the light of experience we shall know how it will work out. If, later on, it is found that some changes might be made I shall be the first to join with hon. gentlemen opposite in suggesting such amendments as experience may dictate. What we are trying to do is not to rush the house to a conclusion. What we are endeavouring to achieve is an orderly, carefully conceived, fully documented opportunity for all to discuss these matters of great importance to the country.
Again, I emphasize that if our experience indicates that what has been done deserves further amendment there will be no delay in providing the house with an opportunity to make the necessary changes, all directed to one end, namely to make parliament stronger, more effective, and more deliberatively able to carry out the task that rests upon it and upon all hon. members of the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: AFRICA-EDUCATIONAL ASSISTANCE TO FRENCH SPEAKING STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make concerning educational assistance to French speaking African states.
The government's attention has been directed to the present needs and to the number and complexity of the difficulties which will confront the emergent nations of Africa in the field of education for some years to come. We have been impressed by their problems and as a result the government has approved in principle the establishment of a Canadian program of educational assistance for the newly independent French speaking African states.
The plan will be entirely separate from any scheme now in existence and should serve to balance Canada's educational assistance program in general. The existing commonwealth education program, while national in character, by its very nature limits the extent of participation of our excellent French speaking institutions and resources. We are confident that these will be used to good advantage in the application of the new plan.
It is proposed that the educational assistance plan for French speaking African states will provide grants of the order of $300,000 annually. Subject to the views of the various parties concerned with the development and execution of this scheme this amount could be applied toward scholarships, the provision of teachers and teacher training or to other types of educational assistance as may seem practicable and desirable.
The countries to which the scheme would be directed are vitally preoccupied with the serious task of improving their educational

facilities and with expanding educational opportunities for their peoples. They have repeatedly expressed their need for scholarships abroad for French speaking students and for French speaking teachers in their own countries. Because of our genuine interest in their welfare and progress and because we share a common language with these new states, Canada is in a unique position to render the type of assistance required. It is therefore the intention of the government to ask parliament to appropriate the funds necessary for this purpose once details have been worked out with the provincial educational authorities.
The new program will result in especially heavy demands on Canada's French speaking educational resources which, like all our educational facilities throughout the country, are already strained. Nevertheless I am confident from past experience and from the expressions of public interest already made regarding this type of venture that when an approach is made the provincial authorities and others concerned in the development and operation of the scheme will respond promptly and willingly. The government therefore intends to seek the co-operation and advice of the provincial educational authorities and the educational organizations and institutions at an early date for the successful implementation of what I am certain the house will agree is a purposeful and timely step.
It is also the government's hope to draw upon the advice and the experience of the United Nations educational, scientific and cultural organizations-better known as UNESCO-in setting up and in operating the new program. A conference sponsored by UNESCO will be held in Addis Ababa next month to examine the educational needs of the African states and to draw up plans to meet those needs in the coming years. It is the government's intention to accept an invitation to send a Canadian observer to these meetings and thus to acquire firsthand knowledge of the educational problems of the area. Information obtained at the conference would eventually be most useful in our own planning for the successful development and execution of the Canadian plan.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the house will be very happy about the announcement which has just been made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. In so far as we on this side of the house are concerned, we have no hesitation in commending the government for this step, which has just been announced, in setting aside the sum of $300,000 as a fund for scholarships.

(Translation):
The Secretary of State for External Affairs will remember that this matter has been discussed more than once in this house, not only by opposition members but by other members as well.
It seems that the decision taken by the government is not only commendable but that it will be welcomed by French universities in the province of Quebec, as well as in other provinces.
In addition, I am particularly glad that the government has decided to confer with provincial authorities regarding the program it intends to submit.
Once again I express our satisfaction to the government. When we reach this item in the departmental estimates, we will take that opportunity to discuss the matter.
I should like to assure the minister right now that we are entirely satisfied with his plan.
(Text):

subsubtopic: AFRICA-EDUCATIONAL ASSISTANCE TO FRENCH SPEAKING STATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, speaking on behalf of this group I wish to say that we heartily endorse this plan announced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in respect of Canada assisting in the educational development and advancement of the French speaking African states. We are quite confident that those teachers who go to these countries will do credit to Canada and will be of assistance to the people they aim to serve. I think this program will further indicate, first, our interest and concern in the welfare and development of the persons in these African states and, second, it will be a happy reflection on our national cultural heritage and its development into the international sphere.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this motion to go into supply gives the opposition another opportunity to raise matters about which it seeks to complain from time to time. Of course, I would have preferred to have this motion put earlier. However, there are events which take place in the house over which neither the opposition nor, for that matter, a private member has control. At the outset, before going into the subject which I desire to submit to the house 90205-6-249
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy on this occasion, I do want to say that from time to time we have repeatedly made the statement and the charge that the main features of the present Conservative administration seem to be confusion, indecision and lack of leadership. It could be easily shown that on more than one occasion that was the position of the government. Certainly, that can be said in the field of national defence. As the house knows, the government is acquiring very expensive equipment, but no decision has yet been taken in so far as the use of nuclear weapons is concerned.
The government is building two Bomarc missile bases in northern Ontario and northern Quebec which, in order to be effective must be equipped with nuclear weapons, but still the decision in so far as those weapons are concerned has not yet been taken. The same can be said in the field of monetary policy. The government refuses to accept any responsibility-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. Evidently we are to have a repetition of what was attempted by the Leader of the Opposition on the last motion to resolve the house into committee of supply. On that occasion the Leader of the Opposition began by talking about a number of subjects before indicating to the house what was to be the specific alleged grievance that was to be the subject matter of his amendment. Already the hon. member for Laurier is into a second subject and appears to be ready to repeat the tactics of the Leader of the Opposition on the last occasion.
You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that when objection was taken at that time you made a ruling and you were quite definite in drawing attention to and, indeed, enforcing the well established rule of the house that on an occasion of this kind an opportunity is given to the opposition to raise a grievance and on such a motion we do not proceed to a second grievance until the first one is disposed of. Other hon. members are entitled to discuss the first grievance before a second one is raised. That is the well established rule and a rule that you enforced on that occasion.
The hon. member has begun by talking about defence questions and now, as a second subject, he apparently proposes to talk about monetary policy. I suggest that if he has chosen to discuss defence as a matter of grievance other hon. members are entitled to submit their views on that subject to the house before any hon. member goes on to raise a second grievance. If the hon. member for Laurier should choose to discuss the second subject he has mentioned, namely, monetary policy, it is quite obvious that has

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy already been the subject of an amendment on a previous occasion on a motion to resolve the house into committee of supply and has been disposed of by decision of the house. Obviously it is not open to the hon. member to raise that subject again on a motion of this kind.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I submit it would be the proper course in seeking to make debates of this kind orderly if the hon. member, who evidently intends to introduce an amendment, were called upon to indicate the nature of that amendment to begin with before entering upon a general review of a number of subjects which is apparently what he is now seeking to do in breach of the rules.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it looked very much as if the Minister of Finance was going to take far more time than I in dealing with a point of order which I submit with deference is not well taken.
With a lot more sense though.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Minister of Finance has referred to several grievances that are being taken up by myself seriatim. That is not the case. I made one passing reference to national defence. Then I went on to another matter as, I submit with deference, I have a perfect right to do. When I come to the matter that I intend to discuss in detail I will indicate to the house what it is and then move an amendment. I say it is not contrary to the rules of the house to do what I have done up to this moment, namely, to make a passing reference to a policy or to a lack of policy on the part of the government. That is all I have done. I have dealt with one such matter and I propose to proceed to deal with another. I submit to you with deference, sir, that surely I have a right to do that in moving an amendment to a motion to go into committee of supply.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon. member for Laurier will agree with me that a supply motion offers an opportunity to debate a specific grievance and that, to avoid the problem of a debate without margins or limits, the practice on supply motions has been to indicate the general area of debate, either by indicating what the amendment is if an amendment is to be moved or by indicating what area the amendment will cover, before proceeding. Otherwise, a problem does arise, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Finance, and did arise on the last supply motion which caused some considerable difficulty because of the reference to a great many subjects which were actually not covered and could not have been covered under the amendment finally moved.

I raise no objection to the hon. member referring to a number of other items. The rule is against debating items which are not germane to the amendment that he proposes to move. I think it would be good practice, as has been established by our proceedings in the past, for the hon. member to indicate at the outset of his speech the area he proposes to cover, just as is done after the amendments are disposed of. A member rises, discusses a specific item of grievance, and is entitled to deal with only one item.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I should like to request direction from you. In dealing with a side issue in passing the hon. member has made a misstatement of fact, and I am wondering what position we are in from the point of view of correcting his misstatement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member wishes to speak to the point of order and indicate that he disagrees with the interpretation of the hon. member for Laurier, he has the opportunity to do so now before the point of order is disposed of. It is not a question of interpretation. The hon. member made the statement, and I copied down his words, that the Bomarc missile requires a nuclear warhead in order to be operative. That is clearly not in accordance with the facts.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry but I misunderstood the hon. member. I thought his intervention related to the point of order and not to the substance of what had been said.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

To come back to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I have no fault to find with the statement you have just made in which you indicated there is nothing objectionable about a general discussion provided the member speaking does not go into detail. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The point is that I had not had the opportunity to deal with any matter because I was interrupted. I was saying that in the field of monetary policy the government refuses to accept any responsibility although-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise again on a point of order. The hon. member in addition to defying your ruling-

speechtext:

234. The ancient doctrine that the redress of grievances should be considered before the grant of supplies is maintained in the House of Commons of Canada.
(1) Whenever an order of the day has been read for the house to resolve itself into the committee of supply or the committee of ways and means, the motion "That the Speaker do now leave the Chair" must be proposed, except on Wednesdays, Thursdays and Fridays as provided by standing orders 56 and 58. The debate in such a case is limited by the rules respecting past decisions, anticipation, sedition, reflections on the Senate-
And so on. The reference, of course, is to "redress of any grievance". I think the fact that the word "grievance" is in the singular 90205-6-249i
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy is significant. I refer the house to a decision of my predecessor in the chair which indicates that a specific matter should be discussed at this time. This decision will be found in Hansard of May 16, 1955, volume 4 at page 3790. I do not wish to take up more time because I think there is perhaps little difference between what I have been saying and what the hon. member for Laurier proposes to do. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think I have any fault to find with your decision, Mr. Speaker. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. member will permit me to interrupt again, may I make this observation.
