I believe that was the substance of my remarks which he cited earlier.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The question I intend to discuss is one having to do with trade. I might as well tell the house that immediately. I say that here there has been the same kind of lack of leadership and the same kind of indecision-
And the same speech.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -that we have seen from time to time on other matters. Certainly that is the case in connection with the report of the royal commission on transportation. That report has been in the hands of the government now for several weeks; and although the matter is one of grave consequence, the government does not seem to be able to make up its mind although there is a strike deadline just ahead of us on May 15 or May 16.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: Has the hon. gentleman any more suggestions-
Order.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext:
-or scattergun objections?

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) asks if I have any more suggestions. I simply say this to the Prime Minister. The responsibility is his. He has in his hands an important document. It seems to me that the house should be entitled at this time if not earlier, to some indication of what the government intends to do. However, we are far from getting such indication. Only this afternoon did we obtain some indication of what the government intends to do in so far as the Freight Rates Reduction Act is concerned. Then again, since there is going to be an amendment to that act, as the Prime Minister has indicated, there must be a statute.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I understood that the hon. member for Laurier does not propose to move an amendment in that field of transportation. It seems to me that, in addition to illustrating his point which I take it was lack of decision on the part of the government, he has gone on to debate the matter and that he should now return to his grievance.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I disagree with you respectfully, Mr. Speaker, I did not go on to debate the matter until after I was asked by the Prime Minister a question as to what suggestions I had to make. My reply was that the responsibility was his. From there I went on to say that here is a statute, the Freight Rates Reduction Act-

speakerposition: Prime Minister
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. What I said was this: What is your next scattergun objection? In other words I was simply referring to the fact that the hon. gentleman is just playing ducks and drakes with the ruling which Your Honour made.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with more care perhaps to what the hon. member for Laurier was saying because I was not thinking of making any interjection. As I recall it, what the hon. member said was that he intends to discuss the matter of trade about which there has been indecision and so on and that this was characteristic of the government. In making his argument he was giving a certain number of analogies. The Chair has ruled over and over again that in argument analogies are certainly in order even if they relate to other matters.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the proposition stated by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillin-gate is unexceptionable. However, the hon. member for Laurier, far from limiting his remarks to an analogy, was making some positive debating assertions about the attitude

of the government, a procedure which to my mind is quite out of order in view of what he has indicated hitherto.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I of course, accept your ruling, Mr. Speaker. However, I contend that if I went beyond the rules, it was certainly under provocation.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is in the field of trade that perhaps there has been the greatest confusion on the part of the government. We all remember the famous trade diversion proposal made by the Prime Minister in July of 1957. It was intended to increase our trade with the United Kingdom. The United Kingdom took the Prime Minister's proposal seriously and in September of 1957 it presented a counter proposal. It presented to the government a free trade proposal which was the only concrete and practical way of attaining the objective expressed by the Prime Minister in July. What was the reaction of the Canadian government to that proposal? In an earlier debate I had occasion to state what the reaction was.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: To misstate it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
However, in effect there is no doubt that the government refused even to consider the proposal of the British government; and in this house, in spite of our repeated demands, we were not successful in getting from the ministers any statement about this proposal. In other words, the proposal of the British government was simply ignored by those who sit opposite me at the moment. Instead of seriously considering the British offer, the government in the fall of 1957 decided to send a trade mission to the United Kingdom. But it was a buying mission, and the slogan then used by the government was "Buy British".
This was in the fall of 1957. However, in the 1958 budget the Minister of Finance decided to increase the tariff on British woollens. They constituted, as the house knows, one of the main export items of the United Kingdom to Canada. That was the answer which was made by the members of the government to those in the United Kingdom who had something constructive to offer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that, having regard to the report of the tariff board upon which we acted, and the condition of the woollen textile industry in Canada, this proposal to the house was not a proper proposal at the time, and he condemns it?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The answer to that question is quite simple and I will be dealing with some aspects of the textile industry later on.
However, the point is that notwithstanding the offer which was made, even although there was a proposal from the British government, the government "upped" the tariff against British woollens. There can be no denial as far as this is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Do you say we
should not have done it?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Later during the session of 1958 the government decided to amend the Customs Act in order to re-establish the system of arbitrary valuations which had been established during the Bennett regime. This legislation gave to the cabinet and the Minister of National Revenue wide arbitrary powers to raise the tariff by order in council. This was not only incompatible with the spirit and the objectives of GATT, but also with our system of parliamentary democracy.
According to the government at that time, the new legislation had become absolutely necessary and essential to protect Canadian industry. However, as a result of strong protests from the governments of the United Kingdom and the United States we have been told that the legislation which was so essential in 1958 has been very seldom applied since.
I think in answer to a question in this house the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan) was unable to say whether or not it had been used, or stated that if so, it had been used very infrequently.
Canadian industry, therefore, has not received the protection it had been led to expect from the government, but none the less ministers have retained the arbitrary powers they should not have in a parliamentary democracy. In 1959-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not yield the floor to my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am rising on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I do not care whether or not the hon. member yields the floor; I am rising on a point of order.
The hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) has purported to attribute a statement to my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Nowlan). The hon. member has not quoted the statement from Hansard, and I say that the statement he has attributed to my colleague is not the statement my colleague made.
My colleague said it had not been necessary to use those powers-
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
That is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The minister has risen to express his disagreement with a statement made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). The practice of the house is that the minister would be allowed to rise and make the correction after the hon. member for Laurier had resumed his seat. I think this is the proper course to follow.
If the hon. member for Laurier yields the floor for the minister to make a correction, that is all very well; but if he does not yield the floor for such purpose, the practice is that such correction of a misstatement or misunderstanding should be made after the hon. member who has the floor has resumed his seat.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have yielded the floor to my hon. friend on several occasions. I do not propose to do so again unless it is in accordance with the rules of the house.
I continue from where I was interrupted to say that in 1959 the government continued to follow a timid, protectionist policy which certainly did not help Canadian industry but was enough to give us a bad reputation in countries outside Canada.
The Minister of Finance continued to appear to be a strong supporter of GATT, in words of course, but how could Canada's words be taken seriously in international meetings when in fact in the fall of 1958 the Minister of National Revenue had violated the very spirit of GATT?
Meanwhile the government expressed its timid approval of the two new trading blocs emerging in Europe, although, as it now appears, it was strongly opposed to a unified European common market. This was a most inconsistent attitude to take.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The government failed to see that the emergence of two separate trading blocs in Europe was not only artificial but also undesirable. It was obvious from the beginning that the formation of the outer seven was mainly a bargaining move intended to bring about a European trade community which negotiations between individual nations had failed to achieve.
The government's confusion, however, became complete in 1960. It accepted, with at least some apparent enthusiasm, a full membership in O.E.C.D., which is supposed to foster European economic unity, but both the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees) threatened to take retaliatory action against the United Kingdom-

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -if the British government accepted the terms required by the common market countries to bring about such economic unity.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not true.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance says that is not true. I hold in my hand a press clipping from the Regina Leader-Post entitled:
Mr. Fleming's protectionist approach to Europe paying lip service to free trade.
This article is dated November 29, 1960.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What was the source?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I said, the Regina Leader-Post. The article continues as fallows:
A highly protectionist frame of mind and intent, based on fear, now stands revealed in two new documents presented by and given the blessing of Canada's Minister of Finance, Donald M. Fleming.
One of the documents, an address delivered by Mr. Fleming to the Canadian industrial editors' association last week at Ste. Adele, Quebec, outlined at length the official government reaction to the new European trading groups.
The article then goes on and states:
Mr. Fleming, of course, reiterates his violent opposition to Britain entering the European common market in any way. He finds it difficult to see how any accommodation which the United Kingdom might make with the "Six" nations "could fail to damage to some degree, and perhaps seriously, Canadian interests".
This article continues:
But by far the most significant words used by Mr. Fleming in both his Ste. Adele address and his Times article, filled in this important detail:
This paragraph is in quotations:
"If," he says, "the more damaging possibilities in fact materialized, if the impact on free entry and commonwealth preferences were far-reaching and if reverse preferences were created against us, there would be Canadians who would claim that the system of commonwealth preferences was at an end".
Earlier the article states:
Mr. Fleming describes such a possibility as a "threat". He sees, if it should come about, an end to the present preferential entry of Canadian goods onto the British market, hitherto so valuable to Canada. He fears especially the possibility of damage to the rate of entry of Canadian agricultural products into Britain.
Then there is this significant paragraph:
"Certainly under such circumstances, the pressures for Canada to embark on closer trade associations with other countries, particularly the United States, would understandably be greatly increased".
Then later on:
From an expressed position of advocating a trade diversion away from the United States, the finance minister within a short space of time has now

come to the position of considering the possibility of adopting a policy which would be quite the reverse.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Rot.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The article continues:
Should it come about, there would be few if any patterns of policy development which could compare with it in the history of Canada.
Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce made no secret about his position when he was in Paris. Here I quote from a clipping from the Ottawa Journal dated December 15, 1960 and datelined Paris:
Unless the European common market substantially reduces its announced tariff schedules affecting imports from Canada, at the GATT negotiations in progress in Geneva Canada will retaliate by increasing its barriers against imports from the six European countries. That warning has been given by trade minister Hees to the European ministers meeting here.
There can be no doubt about that statement, and if it is not accurate I presume the minister will deny it. But that has not been done in this house. Then a new round of negotiations was initiated in Geneva by GATT members, and if the Minister of Finance is sincere in saying he is a strong supporter of trade on a multilateral basis the Canadian delegates at Geneva must surely have presented concrete and bold proposals for freer trade in the world. While these negotiations were going on, however, the Minister of Finance in his supplementary budget took another important step on the road to greater protection with his amendment to the provisions respecting the class or kind of goods made in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I rise to a point of order? It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to make reference to matters which have engaged the attention of the house in previous sessions or to make reference to things which happened outside the house and which are not subject to a decision in the house, but he is now referring to a matter which engaged the attention of hon. members over the past two months, the debate of which was concluded on the third reading of the bill last week. The hon. member has now begun to discuss this matter again and I submit he is out of order.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance is again wasting his breath entirely. I have not started to discuss this subject. I made reference to it, and I have completed my reference. The minister cannot remain in his seat for a moment. When anything is said which concerns his department or which affects him he must rise immediately and protest. I hope he will rise and protest on those occasions when he should do so in accordance with the rules of the house but not otherwise.

I was going on to say, after that statement, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is a great showman. He has shown that on more than one occasion, and so has the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for that matter. But the showmanship of the Prime Minister is in the field of vision whereas, I must admit, the showmanship of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is more real. However, since the calling together of the trade commissioners in Ottawa to meet the businessmen the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been touring the country preaching a "Buy Canadian" campaign. In the fall of 1957 the slogan was "Buy British". Today it is "Buy Canadian", and the great export drive which was begun with such enthusiasm and apparent dynamism not long ago and which received so much publicity last fall seems now to have been entirely forgotten by those who sit on the other side of the house.
What will the next step be? I presume it will come when the Minister of Finance hands down his budget. Once again the Minister of Finance will probably talk about freer trade on a multilateral basis at the beginning of his speech when he refers to the international economic situation and then announce further protective action at the end of his speech just before reaching his final exhortation. At least, this is what the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion) led his audience to expect when he spoke recently in St. Hyacinthe and promised that the textile industry would soon be adequately protected against foreign competition. Did the Minister of Finance read the speech of his colleague the Secretary of State? Did he compare it with the speeches made by the Prime Minister about greater protection for the textile industry against dumping, protection for that industry in the same manner as agricultural products, for instance, are protected against dumping.
I think the Minister of Finance should read what was said by his colleague. There is no doubt that this speech, together with other speeches made by the Prime Minister, adds up to a long list of inconsistencies and contradictions. The examples I have given are not exhaustive. I have not the time to put them all on record in Hansard, but they are none the less impressive. The government has talked one way and acted another. The government has given the indication that it intended to move in one direction while, as a matter of fact, acting in the other way; although its actions, when it did move, have proved of little assistance to those industries which were in need of assistance and which required protection.
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
Meanwhile our export trade has, fortunately, continued to expand. The government cannot take credit for this expansion, which is due not to its policies but to the dynamic economy and growth of western European industry. The increase of 9 per cent in the physical volume of our export trade since 1957 does not justify complacency on the part of the government, and there have been indications of such complacency from time to time. In the first place that expansion has not been fast enough to enable our economy to move ahead or even to retain its position. Moreover, this upward trend may well come to an end when the new trading arrangements in Europe are fully implemented at which time their restrictive features will begin to produce results.
The formation of O.E.C.D. was certainly a step in the right direction. One of the main functions of the new organization was-and I quote:
To achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries while maintaining financial stability.
However, O.E.C.D. will not be able to accomplish very much in that direction if an excessive stress is placed on economic aid functions which annoy many Europeans. Moreover, the new organization can be at best a useful forum for discussion leading to a better co-ordination of economic policies and, in particular, to new trading arrangements within the north Atlantic community. But in order to achieve this most important objective, member countries must decide what trade policy is best for them and try to reconcile their differences in order to pursue a common purpose.
If this is to be done, Canada, in particular, must abandon its present confused and ineffective trade policy. The government must get out of its present dilemma and realize that it is impossible to have at the same time two conflicting trade policies, one of free trade for our export industries and one of high protection for our secondary manufacturing industries.
This basic conflict can be solved only when we become aware of the very important fact that high protection is not the only way and, in the framework of our international obligations, is certainly not the best way of helping our secondary manufacturing industries.
If we were to rely only on a restrictive trade policy to assist this sector of our economy high tariffs and quotas would be necessary. This would mean, of course, that we would have to withdraw from GATT and that our export industries would be exposed to massive retaliation. Such a restrictive policy

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy would be a fatal blow for our export industries and it would not solve the basic difficulties of our secondary manufacturing industry.
The source of those difficulties comes from relatively high production costs resulting from a small domestic market and lack of specialization. High protection, it seems to us on this side of the house, can do very little to remove this basic weakness. At best it could offer only a temporary advantage and give to our domestic industry a larger share of a smaller market resulting from a decline of the export industries.
The only realistic long term solution to the difficulties experienced by our secondary manufacturing industry lies in the direction of free trade. Our domestic industries would then have an easy access to large markets and would be able to specialize. It could produce fewer products in much greater quantities resulting in substantially lower costs of production.
The gradual establishment of free trade would, of course, create transitional problems for our domestic industry. It would have to change its production techniques, modify its equipment and intensify its sales efforts abroad. These transitional problems, however, can be solved if the government is prepared to initiate a special program of assistance to our domestic industries. This should not be difficult because, when one considers what happened in the formation of the common market countries, where the same problems were met, and with tremendous success, one can realize that it can be done. When it is considered that these six countries, two of which have lower tariffs than ours and two others of which have higher tariffs, were able by agreement among themselves to reduce their tariffs to a common denominator [DOT]-there is no doubt that difficulties were encountered in the process-and if it could be accomplished with the results, which we know over there, and give such dynamism and increase to the trade, there is no doubt that similar action could be followed here.
Such a program, as I have outlined in a general way, because I have already put it on Hansard in a more detailed manner in another debate, should be highly flexible and include loans, grants and tax incentives. It should also be carefully planned in consultation with industry in order to be well adapted to the concrete re-adjustments involved. Its large-scale implementation would not create any special financial problems because it would be accompanied by the gradual removal of a tariff burden which is estimated at more than $1 billion annually. We suggest on this side of the house, that this might well
CMr. Chevrier.]

be accomplished either through the reorganization of the Department of Trade and Commerce or by the creation of a new department of industry to implement the plan that has been referred to from time to time in the house.
The program of assistance which I just outlined would solve the basic problems of our secondary manufacturing industry much more effectively than high protection. It has the additional tremendous merit of being perfectly consistent with the best interests of our traditional export industries.
Each generation of Canadians has been tempted by the apparent simplicity of high protection but has found through bitter experience that a restrictive trade policy is not suited to Canadian conditions. Throughout our history, our export trade has been the main dynamic factor of our expansion and prosperity. When our export industries experienced difficulties, as in the second half of the nineteenth century, the whole Canadian economy failed to grow rapidly. When the level of our exports was increasing substantially, as it did most of the time during the present century, we enjoyed over-all rapid expansion.
Thus, sir, the major aim of our trade policy should be to promote exports through freer trade, while enabling our secondary manufacturing industry at the same time to adjust itself to this new environment through the implementation of a special program of assistance. We should, however, be realistic enough to realize that progress toward free trade on a world scale is becoming more and more difficult. The underdeveloped countries are not likely to support such a movement. The Sino-Soviet bloc are opposed to it, and the emergence of other regional trading arrangements have given a new direction to the free trade movement. On the other hand, a free trade arrangement between Canada and the United States alone would be undesirable for us not only for economic but also, and perhaps especially, for political reasons.
The gradual establishment of free trade between the emerging European common market, including the outer seven and the inner six, and North America, seems to be the only realistic objective that we should seek. The unification of the two European trading zones in a broad common market now appears inevitable. It is also highly desirable, and we would not oppose it, provided it is developed within the framework of a North Atlantic free trade area. Such an arrangement would not only make sense for Canada but it would also strengthen all the national economies of the western world and put them in a better position to help the underdeveloped countries, and to meet the

Soviet challenge. Moreover, the creation of this Atlantic trade community would consolidate the political unity of western democracies and give a new purpose to the alliance of the free world.
This great idea of an Atlantic trade community was put forward for the first time by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in December, 1957 in Oslo when he received the Nobel peace prize. He then said:
Now the European nations are launching themselves through the common market and its associated free trade area, on an adventure in the economic unification of peoples that a few years ago would have seemed completely visionary. Is it any more visionary to foresee a further extension of this co-operative economic pattern? Is it not time to begin to think in terms of an economic interdependence that would bridge the Atlantic?
Then again, on January 24, 1958, in a speech made in Vancouver, my leader repeated his suggestion in the following terms:
In short, it seems that the era of gradual tariff reductions through GATT have come to an end. We do not surely wish to replace it by a western Europe and a North America aiming at selfsufficiency. If not, then surely the best alternative, and the best way to meet the Soviet economic and political challenge is an Atlantic freer trade area to complement the European customs union and free trade zone. For Canada, is this not the best way to reduce our economic dependence on the United States while expanding our trade, maintaining our economic development and raising even higher our living standards? This is a challenging prospect and is surely worth serious and immediate consideration, negotiation and planning. Could there be a finer initiative for Canada?
This idea has now received the acclaim and support of most of the western leaders. There is no doubt of the position which Prime Minister Macmillan of the United Kingdom took during his visit to this continent. Not only in Washington, but also in the speech which he delivered to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and during the press conference which he gave here on April 12 the Prime Minister of Great Britain said that the free world must think in terms of creating the largest area of free trade possible and a North Atlantic free trade area should be created. Vice President Johnson, speaking in Paris at the beginning of April, developed the same theme. In an address in Toronto in December, 1960, Mr. Stevenson had this to say:
A working Atlantic community would do more than enhance the basic strength of the west. It would demonstrate to other areas-to Latin America, to Africa, to the Middle East and to India and Pakistan-methods by which political autonomy can be combined with supra-national co-operation.
The West German minister of economic affairs, Mr. Erhard, and of defence, Mr. Strauss, have expressed on several occasions their support for a North Atlantic free trade area.

Mr. Maurice Faure, former French minister of European institutions, said recently:
In my view the answer to European and to NATO problems is the same: at both levels we must outgrow the old-fashioned concept of a mere alliance between sovereign states and work out new patterns of organic unity. European unification and Atlantic co-operation should progress simultaneously. The ultimate goal should be a European federation within an Atlantic confederation.
Mr. Spaak and Van Zealand in Belgium, and the political leaders of the Scandinavian countries, have made statements along the same lines. Therefore, it can be seen that the idea put forward by the Leader of the Opposition in December of 1957 is now widely supported in the North Atlantic countries. The Leader of the Opposition is now suggesting an Atlantic economic conference, at the highest governmental level, for the purpose of laying the foundation for an Atlantic economic community. I submit the government should accept the suggestion and take the lead in calling such a conference.
Instead, the Minister of Trade and Commerce has rejected any idea of Canadian participation in the gradual establishment of an Atlantic free trade area. This he did at a meeting of the Progressive Conservative party in March. "This house regrets the protectionist and inconsistent trade policies of the government and its failure to develop a long term foreign economic policy to enable Canada to participate fully in the challenging new opportunities in the field of international trade by implementing a vigorous program to promote the expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries and by encouraging the development of an Atlantic economic community."

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before I place the amendment before the house I shall be glad to know whether any hon. member wishes to raise any point with respect to the proposed amendment?

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the amendment and I can say immediately that our group intends to support it. We note that according to the statistics our exports have been rising in recent years. However, we contend they have not been rising fast enough to meet our national needs. We have to remember that in order to obtain a satisfactory level of exports they must be at a level adequate enough to pay for the goods and services we import. In addition to paying for the goods and services we import, they must also be enough to meet our payments on our foreign debt and it is to be noted that the level of such payments has been rising with tremendous rapidity of

late. We have to repay to those who invest in Canada not only the basic principal of the investment but also the interest and if equity is involved our economy is expected to return a profit on the investments that outsiders make in our country.
In addition to having to pay by means of exports for the goods and services we import and also our foreign debt, we must also regard our export needs in the light of employment needs in our own country. In the light of world needs, our group denies completely any necessity for unemployment in Canada. However, we realize at once that our exports have a lot to do with the level of employment and unemployment in Canada and we realize that we have to export an ever-growing proportion of our wealth if we are going to provide employment for all those in Canada who would like to work.
I note that according to the official statistics our over-all deficit in 1959 was $1,429 million. This is a matter of very serious concern. I agree at once that the objective of the amendment is a good one. However, we contend that in Canada we should be producing what we are able to produce economically, and the attainment of that objective will mean changes in our economic structure. We will have to make a selection of products. We will have to make up our minds what we are able to produce economically in Canada in relation to the rest of the world and we will have to concentrate on those products rather than attempting to protect the man with a greenhouse who is trying to produce bananas for Canadian consumers. I say at once that whole industries need not be sacrificed, that rather we should decide now that we must give up the production of certain products because they may be uneconomical and their continued production may be against the long term national interest.
At this time I should like to compliment the Canadian producers of industrial machinery. I believe they have realized that their continued prosperity depends on specialization and, having regard to the recession and all other factors, I believe they are doing relatively well because they have taken into account the fact that we can compete only by specializing and that we cannot compete very successfully on the basis of nationalism which is outdated in the economic world of today.
I should like to express my disappointment at the failure of Canadian industries generally to realize that they have to adjust in order to survive. If we want to have a proper approach we must realize that we are not an island by ourselves in the world today. We have to accept the world as it is and if our industries want to survive they will only

survive provided they are willing to adjust to economic realities and attune their operations accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I was a little bit surprised that the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) appeared as the leading spokesman on behalf of the Liberal party in the debate dealing with the subject of trade. Alleged Lack of Trade Policy amendment in its reference to expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries. Had the hon. member for Ottawa West been responsible for this amendment, I believe he would have omitted this reference of particular concern to the expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries. The hon. member for Laurier has always been well known as a spokesman for the textile industry which, as we all know, is under a severe handicap, as it has been for a considerable number of years. However, our group recognizes the fact that our needs in the field of international trade cannot be successfully resolved until we have resolved the problem of unemployment in Canada within our own national borders. I agree at once that we are unable to resolve the complications of this problem until we build up adequate markets that will relieve us of the curse of unemployment. We appreciate at once that the immediate way of resolving the problem of unemployment is to enhance our obvious home market by giving our people adequate purchasing power. However, in addition to that, much can be done to enhance our markets abroad. I should like to quote, merely for the record, a submission made today to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his cabinet by the national unemployment lobby committee. On this particular matter it reads as follows, at page 9:
More should be done to promote trade. We should seek to expand our trade with all countries. Trade representatives should go to countries where our trade up to now has done poorly. A permanent trade commission should be established to visit all countries in turn. There should be a Canadian export bank to help exporters, with loans guaranteed by the government. Long term loans and technical assistance should be extended to so-called underdeveloped countries on a still larger scale; the loans should be at a nominal rate of interest, or interest free. Capital goods, which Canadian industry is quite able to make if allowed and helped to do so, should be an important part of our aid program.
Many eminent people, here and abroad, have suggested that Canada and other countries should use 1 per cent of their gross national product for foreign aid. This would mean $360 million for Canada. We doubt that the present total is even one third of that.
May I only interject that our present total is not even a fifth of that amount. The submission continues:
Mutual aid is certainly the right way to describe this assistance, since it helps the countries giving it as well as those receiving it.

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy which I understand met with the government today. We ought to realize that our particular problems would disappear if we had a policy of full employment. I have read wth a great deal of interest the suggestion of Dr. Hugh Keenleyside. Dr. Keenleyside advocates our entering into an agreement with the United States of America for a selective integration of production. To put it very bluntly, if the United States insist on making automatic washers for the whole North American continent, we might agree to that if they would allow us to make automatic dryers for the whole North American continent.
If the United States want to manufacture large cars for the whole North American continent, they might be persuaded to agree to our manufacturing small cars to satisfy the whole North American market.

Mr. Speaker, the subamendment which has just been moved and the motion moved by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) are both very welcome to the government because I do not know of any area less favourable for members of the opposition to attack than that which has been chosen by the opposition today.
The main motion, which expresses regret at what it calls the protectionist and inconsistent policies of the government, is, in itself, completely inconsistent. It purports to speak on the one hand of a free or freer trade area within the Atlantic economic community and in the same breath it expresses regret because, it says, the government has failed to promote the expansion of secondary manufacturing industries in Canada. These two courses are contradictory and represent opposite ends of the economic pole.
At no time has any government put forth a greater effort to extend trade than this government has done and we shall continue to put forward that effort. We are very anxious to expand trade throughout, not only the Atlantic community, but the whole world and we shall continue to press our efforts in the future to the same degree as we have in past years.
However, I wish to say that supporters of the government will vote against this amendment, since it constitutes a straight vote of no confidence in the government, and if it were carried the government would be out of office. We know that the people are too
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy well pleased with the service which this government is giving, for a chance to be taken of disappointing them at this time.
Canadian trade policy has been developed over many years by successive governments, as we all know, and today it represents the best judgment of the governments of the past and of the present government in the light of economic and political conditions which have existed over the past four years. The government is fully aware that new economic and trade developments are taking place throughout the world, and has been examining its course of action closely for months past. The fact that no precipitate action has been taken to date is a measure of the difficulty of the problem, and the importance of the policy decisions as they are ultimately resolved. I can assure the house, however, that I will recommend to my cabinet colleagues free or freer trade, or the joining by Canada of any economic trade grouping, whenever I am convinced that such a step is not only in the best interest of export groups, but of the Canadian economy as a whole.
Hon. members will know that for months past detailed negotiations have been going on in Geneva to ensure the most favourable terms of access for Canada's exports to the common market. Within the next few days the second phase of the tariff conference in Geneva will begin. The major trading nations of the GATT will be entering into negotiations for the mutual reduction of tariffs, the first such negotiations since 1956. Apart from Canada the leading trading countries participating are the United States, the common market, and the United Kingdom.
These negotiations represent part of the machinery by which we hope to maximize international trade.
Senior officials of my department have been in attendance at Geneva constantly since last August when these negotiations commenced, and will be continuing in these negotiations until they are completed later this year.
I am keeping in close touch with the progress of the negotiations, and I might tell the house the assistant deputy minister of my department is returning to Canada on Wednesday this week to report fully to myself and my officials on the current status of these important discussions.
This government has also seized the opportunity of establishing the closest working relationship with the European countries of both the Six and the Seven by joining the organization for economic cooperation and development, O.E.C.D. Canada was the first country to ratify the O.E.C.D. convention signed last December. The emergence of the

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy two trading blocs in Europe was one of the major reasons for the creation of this forum for continuous consultation in the economic and trade policy field among the countries in Europe and North America.
Let me say once again, Mr. Speaker, that the trade policy of this government is neither protectionist nor inconsistent. Our policy is simply this, to maximize trade in every commodity in every possible market and by this means to provide employment for as many Canadians as possible.
Let us look at the record but before doing so let me make sure that we are talking about the same things. References are constantly made, and have been made in this house today, about the Canadian deficit balance. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Regier) referred to a deficit in 1959 of $1,429 million inferring presumably that this was a trade imbalance. In actual fact, the trade imbalance for 1959 was $368 million, according to the dominion bureau of statistics' publication "Review of Foreign Trade" and in 1960 the trade imbalance had been reduced to $97 million representing the lowest unfavourable trade balance figure in the last six years.
I gave the d.b.s. figures.

In January, 1961 this figure was increased by 8.4 per cent over the previous record January of last year. The facts do not seem to bear out the concerns of the opposition.
The amendment proposed by the opposition would appear to leave the impression that Canada's trade with the countries of Europe is lagging. In fact Canada's trade with this area of the world is going ahead by leaps and bounds. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I would remind the house that this government and my department are adopting every possible aggressive means to promote Canada's trade both at home and abroad. In December last we called home the trade commissioners from all posts abroad for a three-week conference with Canadian businessmen designed to stimulate the interest and knowledge of Canadian businessmen and to acquaint anew our trade commissioners with current business conditions and possibilities for Canadian export trade. The house will know that this conference was a great success and has excited the interest of Canadian businessmen as never before. In the two months since the trade com-misioners returned to their posts over 350 new selling agencies have been established for Canadian manufacturers abroad, and more than 2,000 new agencies are under active negotiation at this very moment. We are very hopeful that these new agencies will stimulate a great deal of additional trade during the months ahead and, as I have said, in the only month for which figures are available since the conference was held, our actual trade was up by a very satisfactory 8.4 per cent.
The recent export finance facility which was introduced by this government, in cooperation with the Canadian chartered banks has already provided a stimulus to export trade. Since the announcement of this new facility last December Canadian capital goods' manufacturers have exhibited keen interest, and have been placed in the position of being able to quote on over $200 million worth of extra business that would not have been possible previously, except for the provision of this joint export financing arrangement.
Naturally Canadian manufacturers must be competitive in tough world markets, but the financing facility now available is the equal of that of any other country both in terms and in cost, and is superior to most.
Our trade commissioners, and my department, will continue to do everything in our power to help our producers make export sales and expand our export markets so that as many Canadians as possible may have jobs replacing the products that are sold. However, salesmen can only accomplish so much. There is a big job to be done by producers in this country as well. I have pointed that out on numerous occasions, and will do so again now, because I think it is important to know where the responsibility lies in providing jobs for our people.
As I have said, our salesmen are working in every possible way they can to make sales, both at home and abroad. Our trade commissioners have indicated to them that they

will do everything in their power to make the contacts, give them the information they need, and act as interpreters, if necessary. In fact, our trade commissioners will do everything except actually sign an order, and that, of course, must be done by the firm itself.
We in this country, as in the United States, are up against very serious competition from countries which, until recently, were our markets. I refer to the countries of western Europe which, in many cases, were devastated by war, but have made a remarkable comeback since that time. They have done so by co-operation between management and labour, in order to get costs down, and improve design and quality. By these actions which they have taken, they have put competitive products on all the markets of the world, and are competing very seriously in the Canadian market, and as a result have had a serious effect on employment in this country.
As a first step in trying to bring about the same kind of co-operative effort here in Canada, that they have achieved in western Europe, to provide jobs for their people-they
have achieved full employment over there____
we have called together recently two very important conferences here in Ottawa. The first was a labour-management conference, consisting of the representatives of the top 15 labour unions in Canada, and the heads of the 15 top management organizations in Canada, such as the Canadian chamber of commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian automobile chamber of commerce, the Canadian export association, and so on. This meeting was a very successful one, and a steering committee, with a joint chairmanship composed of the heads of the Canadian congress of labour and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, was brought into being, and is planning future meetings. We are very hopeful that this will have a real effect in bringing about in Canadian industry the same kind of co-operative spirit that has proved so useful in Europe.
Five days after that conference, and one day before its counterpart in the United States had its first meeting, we had the first meeting of the Canadian productivity council, made up of representatives as members will know, of labour, management, primary industries, the public, the government and agriculture. As in the case of the labour-management conference, this was also a very successful meeting indeed.
The purpose of these groups is, in various fields, to bring about the kind of co-operative effort which, in Europe, has paid off in such large measure, and to bring about the production in Canada of products that will sell
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy in Europe, and here, as well as around the world, so that Canadians can have jobs replacing the products that move off the retailer's shelf. If a product does not sell, then people cannot have jobs making replacements for it. The problem is as simple as that.
We have the big job of getting labour, management and the government to combine and work together in the way they have in Europe, in order to produce products that will sell, and, as a result, provide jobs for our people. If we do the kind of things they have done in Europe, and we are trying to persuade these groups that it is necessary to do so, we can have the same kind of full employment in Canada, just as soon as we decide to work for it in the way they worked for it over there, and we will achieve it in the way they have achieved it.
Mr. Speaker, it was interesting this afternoon to hear the member for Laurier make reference to the new attitude of the Liberal party toward the question of trade. I am interested to learn that they are now completely in favour of free trade. I was interested, as I am sure all hon. members of this house were, to read in the Toronto Daily Star of April 15 an article appearing under the heading "Pearson Asks Free Trade Era". That article began as follows:
"Canada should jump with both feet" into the project of creating an Atlantic free trade area embracing the United States, Britain, Canada and European nations, Hon. Lester B. Pearson, national Liberal leader, told a press conference yesterday-
I think it will be interesting for the house to take a look at what free trade with the United States will mean for the average Canadian, because that is exactly what the Liberal party, as specified by the Liberal leader, is calling for, and would be brought into effect if this country ever had the misfortune of having a Liberal government again in the future. I will outline what the result would be of free trade with the United States, for which that party on the other side of the house is calling.
The industries in the United States have, of course, a market ten times the size of the Canadian market. Their factories are, therefore, able to produce on a much larger scale than ours, with consequent savings and lower costs. If there were free trade between our two countries, as the Leader of the Opposition said his party would bring about if it were in power sometime in the future, the United States factories would simply increase their runs by 10 per cent and pour their goods into Canada at prices against which many Canadian producers could not compete. The result would undoubtedly be the closing down of a great many Canadian factories;

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy mass unemployment; and the resultant hardship for hundreds of thousands of our people, who are today holding down good jobs, and who would be put out of work. I say this is a very strange course of action to be favoured by a party which professes great concern for those who are unemployed.
This afternoon the hon. member for Laurier said that the Liberals are opposed to my urging Canadians to "Buy Canadian". Just what does "Buy Canadian" mean? If Canadian people buy Canadian goods they will provide jobs for Canadian people producing more of those products when they move off the retailer's shelves.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: On a question of privilege, at no time did I indicate to the house or to anyone else that I was opposed to the "Buy Canadian" campaign to which the minister refers. What I did say was that the government was inconsistent in 1957 in advocating a policy of "Buy British" and in 1960 or 1961 advocating a policy of "Buy Canadian".

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
There is no inconsistency whatsoever. If at a time of unemployment such as this any Canadian advocates to his fellow Canadians that they should buy the products manufactured by their fellow Canadians, then I would say he is advocating a good sensible policy aimed at the good of the Canadian people, aimed at putting Canadians to work producing products that would otherwise come in through loopholes in the backdoor that the Liberal party advocated for nine consecutive days in the debate on the class or kind legislation.
We are in favour of Canadians having jobs here in Canada. We are not in favour of, instead of Canadians having jobs in Canada, people having those jobs in Birmingham, Turin, Toledo and Detroit. We want as many Canadians a possible to have jobs here producing Canadian products for Canadians and overseas consumption so that we can have full employment. That is what our policy is and we are proud of it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the minister a question? How can he be so proud of that policy when there are over 700,000 people unemployed?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I have tried to outline to the hon. member and to other hon. members this evening one of the main reasons why a large number of Canadians are unemployed. It is the same reason that a large number of people are unemployed in the United States today. They are unemployed because a great many countries, particularly western European countries, for about 10 years after the war had to come to us to buy products which

they needed because they had literally no way to produce them. Their factories had been devastated. They had no production then. They needed the goods; they came to us and bought them at almost any price we wanted to ask. This was the situation. By hard work, by co-operation, by management, labour and government sitting down and working together they were able to produce goods which are very competitive, good in design and quality and very competitive in price, and they are taking sales away from Canadian and United States products all around the world. It is up to us and United States to realize it. We talked to their ministers while we were in Washington. They are up against exactly the same problem. That is why they set up a productivity council. They are just as worried as we are, and they are working just as hard as we are to try to overcome this great handicap.
We have to get down to the position where we can produce products which are just as desirable to the people throughout the world, as the people of western Europe have been able to do in 15 years. As soon as we do that, we shall have full employment and we shall not get full employment by negative speeches such as the ones which were delivered today and have been delivered all during this session by members of the opposition, tearing down, trying to create lack of confidence, trying to create a picture of doom and gloom, trying to give an idea to the people of Canada that it is a bad time to invest, that people should not build factories, they should not enlarge their inventories because things do not look so good, unemployment is bad, things are gloomy in the country. This is the contribution that members of the opposition are making, and it is not the kind of contribution that any Canadian who is proud to call himself a Canadian should be making at this time. We should be all getting together and putting our shoulders to the wheel, as the Europeans do and did. That is how they put themselves right at the top of the heap after being down in the ashes 15 years ago.
As I say, it upsets the Liberal party to hear us advocate "Buy Canadian", so that Canadians can have jobs producing more of those products, because they do not want jobs for Canadians. Why do they not want jobs for Canadians? Because the more Canadians are employed the happier they will be at the next election. If Canadians are unhappy they might vote for the Liberal party, as members of the opposition hope they may do, and therefore they are trying to create a picture of gloom, doom, chaos and despair in the minds of Canadian people so that they can

say, "Vote us in and we will set everything right". The Canadian people are not going to be fooled any more at this election than they were at the last election.

No, they were not fooled at the last election; they were very well pleased with what they got at the last election and they are going to be satisfied with what they get at the next one because they are going to get another Conservative government and they are going to get a lot of good legislation.
From what I have said, Mr. Speaker, I think it is pretty obvious what hon. members of the Liberal opposition have been up to all during this session. They have been against anything that would create jobs; they are against anything that will give employment to Canadians. What they want are things that will give employment to people in other countries. They are all for people in other countries. They want them to pour cheap goods into Canada to put Canadians out of work and to have mass unemployment, so that they can go to the people at the next election and say, "Elect us and we will save you from your doom". That is the kind of deal they are trying to put over to the Canadian people. The Canadian people are not going to go for it. They are once again going to recognize that their hope lies in electing a Conservative government under the greatest Prime Minister that ever held office in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I think you have ruled already that when a member finds that a misstatement has been made by a previous speaker he should take the first opportunity immediately after that speech to correct that misstatement, and that is what I want to do. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has stated and based his whole speech on a statement made by the Leader of the Opposition, in which he said that our leader advocated a policy of free trade between Canada and the United States. At no time has the Leader of the Opposition, nor have I in my remarks today, stated anything to that effect. What I did state, by putting on the record the position of the Leader of the Opposition and of the Liberal party, was the advocacy of an Atlantic alliance; that is, a free trade area of the western European countries, Canada and the United States, but not Canada and the United States alone. I made it quite clear this afternoon that economic union with the United States would be undesirable for us politically and otherwise.

speechtext: Then, Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know what question has been put to me but there seems to be at least three in the statement made by the minister. What I say in answer to the minister's question is that an Atlantic alliance can be formed among the western European countries, Canada and the United States in the same manner as a common market was formed among the six countries of western Europe and was a success.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with a great deal of attention to the speech just delivered by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees). All we heard was a lot of words which might properly have been spoken not only during an election but some time in the 1930's. This is what we object to.
It would have been far more interesting had the Minister of Trade and Commerce chosen to speak on the government's trade policy and given the house some indication that the government is aware that there have been tremendous changes in the world which make Tory protectionist trade policies completely obsolete. I find it rather strange, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is a relatively young man, has such outmoded and antiquated ideas and theories on trade and commerce.
Hon. members will agree, I believe, that one of the most acute and urgent problems facing the government is that of trying to fit Canada and her high cost economy into a rapidly changing and increasingly competitive world market. The international picture in the field of trade is becoming more and more complex and it is difficult indeed at this stage to forecast what that picture will be 10 or 20 years from now. Yet, Mr. Speaker, if Canada is to find and adopt an advantageous and useful role in this increasingly important field of trade, it will have to adjust its sights not on short-run expediencies which can be but temporary but on an over-all long-run commercial policy which will best serve Canada's interests and be in keeping with the present trends of international trade.
There has been a profound evolution in our concept of international trade within the past

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy 50 years. The old pattern of international trade and the protectionist trade policies of the empire era have long since been discarded and new trade relationships and policies adopted to meet new world situations. Within the past 15 years some 38 nations of the world have attained their political independence and along with their sovereignty went the responsibility of bolstering their economies which they are rightly seeking to do by the processing in their own countries of their raw materials and marketing of the products.
The rest of the world could not be and was not indifferent to the impact that this evolution has had on the international trade picture and the necessity and advantage for all to aid these new nations to stabilize their respective economies. The commonwealth trade preferences, the multilateral trade agreements such as GATT, the international monetary fund, the international bank for reconstruction and development, the Colombo plan, the United Nations technical assistance fund, all were organized to meet the new problem, and we can best judge the success of these endeavours by imagining what would have happened, both in terms of world economics and world politics, had we failed to keep up to new world demands.
Although we have cause to take some satisfaction from what has been done, it would be wrong and dangerous to imagine that the problem of trade has been solved. One has only to recall that not so very long ago we were greatly concerned with the economic plight of, and took steps to bolster, the economy of western Europe. Since then, a relatively few years, the recovery of western Europe and that of Japan have been so outstanding that not only have they increased competition in the international market but they have in fact disturbed, if not disrupted, some of our own home markets.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, the problem of world trade has not been solved but on the contrary we stand on the threshold of a new era in the field of international relationships and trade, and Canada with her high cost economy, her alarming unfavourable trade balances and her urgent need to export cannot afford to lag behind with the government's outmoded, ineffective and unimaginative thinking on international trade.
There is a marked reluctance on the part of the government, if not in accepting the revolutionary changes in the international trade picture, certainly in attuning its thinking and its policies to trends which in recent years have become clear-cut. Since 1935 there has been throughout the world a gradual lowering of trade barriers, the abandonment of bilateral trade arrangements and a continuous movement toward multilateral and

freer trade. It is absolutely useless for the government to try to fight this world trend toward freer trade by attempting to camouflage its trade restrictive policies behind a barrage of administrative red tape as it did in the amendments to the class and kind provisions of the Canadian tariff recently. That is the type of thinking that will not only isolate Canada from the current international trade movement but will make favourable trade negotiations with other countries impossible and ultimately jeopardize Canada's badly needed export trade.
Another example of the application of traditional Tory protectionist policy and the government's refusal to acknowledge and accept the new concept of world trade was the backing away by the government in 1958 from an offer to establish a free trade area between Canada and the United Kingdom. Nor has the government since 1958 to this day decided to scrap its traditional trade policies and thinking, which are not only obsolete but are harmful to our economy at this very crucial time. Not so long ago the Minister of Finance suggested to the United Kingdom government that it should not join the common market; otherwise Canada would be forced to take appropriate steps in retaliation. No doubt the United Kingdom government would have been impressed and alarmed at this Victorian threat some years ago but under the present world situation the minister's suggestion received the consideration it deserved, and it appears inevitable now that the United Kingdom will join the common market.
The best gauge by which to measure the depth and the scope as well as the consequences of the political and economic changes in the world and the proof that Canada will have to adopt more realistic, more imaginative and more practical trade policies are the fact that Great Britain, the mother of parliaments, the emblem of sovereignty and independence, may judge it necessary to sacrifice a part of that independence in order to maintain its economic stability in the face of changed world conditions. We cannot imagine, Mr. Speaker, how much thought, how much reflection, how much consideration must have been given by the United Kingdom to that extremely weighty problem, but we can imagine fairly well how irritatingly naive must have sounded the Minister of Finance's advice and threat at such a crucial moment in the history of Great Britain.
The United Kingdom must, just as Canada must, seek to protect and even defend its economic security as well as the welfare of its people by taking whatever measures are deemed appropriate to cope with new and

challenging economic and political problems on a world scale. The western world in the past 15 years, in order to establish lasting world peace on the basis of understanding and co-operation between the nations of the world, has spared no efforts, no amount of ingenuity and no amount of money to avert a catastrophic third world war. With the United Nations, NATO and SEATO we have succeeded so far in avoiding a third world war and have at least retarded the communist military aggression in Europe and Asia. But Mr. Speaker, who would dare claim that we have enjoyed during these past years a state of even comparative peace? Who would dare assert that the tensions and strifes of the cold war are limited only to occasional military skirmishes, political jockeying for position, the nuclear arms race, the missile and space travel races? What about the world economics race which is more fundamental, a race in which we are handicapped because of the diametrically opposed principles on which western and communist economies are based?
We have sought to unite the western nations in military alliances. We have built up military defences around the world and we have been so busy in keeping the U.S.S.R. from gaining any military advantage over us that we apparently have lost sight of the fact that the real ace up the communist sleeve is their basic economic advantage over us.
The western countries have done little or nothing to bridge this gap and to prepare defences in the event of an economic war which Mr. Khrushchev himself warned us would inevitably be launched. Very little success has been achieved in uniting the western countries in an economic alliance which might be able to offset whatever economic advantage the U.S.S.R. might have over us. Mr. Speaker, it is because an economic war could achieve what the communists have set up as their dedicated objective whereas an all-out nuclear war obviously could not do so, that I am convinced that the western nations most vulnerable spot in their fight against communist domination lies in the field of world economics; and strangely enough, that is the field in which there is the least unity, the least co-operation and the least planning among the nations of the western world.
It is no doubt because of a lack of appreciation of the full impact of present economic and political changes, because of a too narrow and too short view of the international trade problem and because of a continued and incomprehensible underestimation of the Soviet threat and because of the blind adherence to obsolete traditional trade policies and political expediency that governments
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy like this government fail to see in the common market and the free trade area the embryo of greater economic unity, co-operation and strength for the western world. I cannot help but feel that in the minds of many people and of many nations the common market and even the free trade area are considered as discriminatory and restrictive trading blocs and are looked upon as a potential danger to their own export markets.
In the light of present world problems I believe it is wrong for Canada and other nations to consider the common market only in terms of the short-run effects on some of their European exports. If indeed the world situation warrants, as indeed it does, the United Kingdom along with other European nations taking unprecedented and revolutionary steps to meet new challenges effectively, surely Canada cannot expect to meet those same challenges as well as the higher cost economy problem which she has without making some readjustment at least in her export trade.
The common market and the free trade area must not be looked upon in the very narrow, negative and indeed provincial light in which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) views them. These organizations are to me unprecedented and necessary experimentation in the field of world economics not only toward freer trade but toward an essential economic unity and co-operation which we must achieve not only in Europe but among the nations of the western world if we are to meet successfully the challenge of a changing world economy as well as to withstand the pressures of an economic war with the U.S.S.R. and her satellites.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, Canada cannot and must not continue to look upon these organizations in an unfavourable light and to remain isolated and aloof from the tremendous effort and movement that is being made to meet the world problems and challenges of this generation. On the contrary, in the light of Canada's trade deficits and her increased difficulty in competing in her own home markets as well as in foreign markets, because of the disruption of traditional trade relationships, because of the possibility of increased economic competition from the Soviet union and her satellites and because of the paramount necessity of aiding the underdeveloped nations of the world, Canada cannot afford to be without a definite, well-thought-out, long range foreign economic policy. The stakes are too high and the situation too tense for Canada to continue to indulge, as she is now doing, in off the cuff, hit-or-miss trade policies, in apologetic but none the less restrictive trade measures with all her hopes
