Alleged Lack of Trade Policy of solving her problems pinned on the loud-talking high pressure salesmanship of the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, the importance and consequences to Canada of world economics warrants the adoption of a definite Canadian foreign economic policy which should be based on a thorough study and understanding of present world problems and should contain both long range and short range measures to cope with these problems. Surely, under present conditions a Canadian foreign economic policy should be given at least the same consideration and importance as is given to foreign affairs policy and indeed more coordination and planning than are now being given to national defence policy. Certainly the long range measures of a sound Canadian foreign economic policy should include not only the acceptance of the European common market and the free trade area as the basis of a trade-promoting endeavour and not a trade-inhibiting endeavour but this long range policy should also include a sincere effort and leadership on the part of Canada to extend the membership and principles involved in these two organizations to a wider North Atlantic economic alliance as a first step to reaching economic unity and co-operation in the whole of the western world.
No one, of course, doubts the necessity and the advantage of aiding the underdeveloped countries at a crucially important point of their economic history. But how will the western world be able to give the necessary assistance and protection to these new economic entities if the western world is plagued with economic problems of its own and is further weakened by a lack of unity and co-operation in the strategically important field of economics?
It would appear to me, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's foreign economic policy should be to support and encourage the principles involved in these European economic associations and seek to extend the application of these principles to Canada and the other North Atlantic countries, in order to strengthen our own economies in the North Atlantic area so as to be in a far better position to be able to help the newly independent countries stabilize their own economies.
It would be most unfortunate if Canada and other countries, particularly the underdeveloped countries, should look on the common market or the free trade area as discriminatory and inward looking when in fact both are laying the basis for freer trade on a world scale and at a time when the economic principles being experimented with in these organizations might be the only basis on which we can hope to achieve stability in
[Mr. Cardin.l

world economics without having to sacrifice our economic and political ideologies.
One would have thought that the Minister of Finance would have been ready and eager to attend the recent meeting of the O.E.C.D. instead of going there backwards and reluctantly. One would have thought that he would have taken the lead in putting teeth into the O.E.C.D. so that it might have some chance of success in co-ordinating world economies, in achieving economic growth and employment in member countries and in contributing to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral non-discriminatory basis which, as we all know, are the aims of the O.E.C.D. These aims are excellent and timely but how can they be successfully achieved if the organization has no authority to carry out its objectives?
Surely we have learned the lesson at the United Nations, that the best aims and objectives, the best motives and intentions are useless without the authority for carrying them out. Admittedly, under the circumstances, it would have been difficult, if at all possible, for the United Nations to have been given the authority it needed to carry out its objectives.
However, this is not the situation among the member nations of O.E.C.D., most of whom belong either to the common market or the free trade area, and all of whom are desperately concerned and eager to contribute toward a more stable world economy and are at the same time dedicated to the preservation of our western ideologies.
Canada could and should have taken some initiative in trying to give O.E.C.D. the authority it must have if it is to co-ordinate the economies of its members and help the underdeveloped countries develop their economies.
Most of the economies of the underdeveloped countries, as hon. members know, are based on two or three basic products, on the stability of which depend the whole of their respective economies.
Canada and the western nations have contributed large sums of money to help these underdeveloped countries help themselves. Most of these countries have used this aid very judicially. However, the fact remains that any artificial fluctuations in the prices of these relatively few commodities means that the whole economic structure of these nations could be destroyed, and whatever aid may have been given them would be wasted.
We have examples in the past where the U.S.S.R. has tampered with the price of commodities, as she did with tin, aluminium and asbestos. We can expect that the U.S.S.R.

will continue to employ very questionable trade practices with the uncommitted countries for political purposes.
Canada could and should have tried to devise some method by which O.E.C.D. might have at least made these unacceptable trading methods less dangerous by making them public, if not protecting the underdeveloped nations or any other nation from these artificial price fluctuations or very questionable trading practices.
O.E.C.D. is not now in a position to cope with this problem among the others they face. My point is that Canada could and should give leadership in making O.E.C.D. a strong economic organization, western style, and, while adhering to the principle of democracy, establish a much needed unity, co-ordination and stability of the economy of the western world.
This is the type of role Canada could play in achieving world economic stability if this government had a real economic policy in relation to the rest of the world.

Mr. Speaker, we have again seen quite a lot of action in this house today. I suggest first of all, sir, that the subsequent motion which the opposition moved in supply did not do them any more good than their performance heretofore.
They have chosen to come forward again with a grievance with regard to trade at a time when Canada's position in world trade never had a more active champion than the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Hees). They have chosen to come forward with this grievance at a time when our trade is at a level which we would like to see maintained at all times in Canada and which, unfortunately, throughout a great many years of Liberal rule was lost almost completely.
One of the first things about which the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) again rose and spouted was the British free trade offer. Unfortunately, for the last few minutes of his speech I was called out of the house and did not hear whether the Liberals accepted the British free trade offer. Do they believe in it? Would they have accepted it had they been in office? Does his industrial riding know that the British free trade offer was a manufacturing free trade offer only and had nothing to do with agricultural products?
Does the hon. member for Laurier have any idea about agricultural produce and how it is supported in England, in the outer seven or the inner six? I do not think he has; I do not think anybody in the Liberal party has any idea about trade or trading. They sold Canada's birthright. They sold it year after
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy year. They gave it away to the British many years ago in the British wheat agreement. That was the time we in western Canada started to doubt these people. That was the time we started to believe they would tell us anything to become re-elected. Fortunately for them there was a war; there was Korea, and they maintained power.
However, this question of trade is only one of the means they have used to try to divide this country. They have got up on the rooftops and in this house and spouted their free trade doctrine. I defy any one of them to tell me what it is, because they do not know. It is a myth and a figment of their imagination. There is no such thing as free trade.
Ask our farmers about free trade. Ask them where they can buy, for instance, a diesel tractor manufactured in England, or even in the United States, at a lower price than we are paying in Canada, and which is selling in those countries at a lower price.
We have no duty against tractors, and yet we even take into consideration the question of freight rates. Can we in western Canada, or anywhere else in this country, buy a tractor from these countries at the retail price plus freight? This is free trade. We cannot do it. Of course we cannot, because the manufacture of these tractors is controlled by international companies. Then where does free trade come in?
What about the British free trade offer, this great figment of the Liberal imagination? Do the textile workers in my hon. friend's constituency think it would help them? Do the manufacturing and industrial workers in any of the industrial cities right across Canada think it will help them, with our smaller market? It would not help them at all.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What are you doing for the textile workers?
We have done a great deal under the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, and if the hon. member will just bear with me a moment-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You put 35,000 of them out of jobs.

-I will educate him a little with regard to subsidies. We in western Canada, Ontario and Quebec have a problem with regard to hogs. We have thought about this problem a great deal, even though my hon. friend may not have done so.
We want our farmers to be able to sell their produce at a reasonable price. A year or so ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton and the former minister, now the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Harkness),
3954	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy persuaded the British to admit 25,000 tons of pork into England. I suggest to my hon. friend that he look at some of the English papers published at that time to see the reaction in the British House of Commons and in Britain itself, the very mother of the commonwealth, with regard to the importation of a little bit of pork from Canada.
What did these people say? They were up in arms about it. Why? Because they, too, wanted to produce a little bit of pork. What is the attitude of the British government toward their farmers? This is why their free trade offer was a manufacturing free trade offer, and this is something hon. members should remember.
The subsidies in Britain vary from year to year. Every agricultural product which is produced in Britain is subsidized, as it is in every other country in the outer seven. One of the greatest problems the countries in the inner six have had to face is the whole question of subsidy on agricultural produce.
Just for the record, in England the subsidy now paid on a bushel of wheat is seven shillings. I am sure my hon. friends can mentally convert that into dollars very quickly. The subsidy on oats and barley is five shillings to 15 shillings. The subsidy for plowing land and putting it into cultivation is seven per acre. One third of the cost of drainage and one third of the cost of fertilizer is subsidized. The subsidy for clearing old woodland and putting it into cultivation is 15 per acre. The subsidy is eight per head for calves that reach the age of six to nine months. Other subsidies are paid on eggs, other livestock and pork.
My hon. friend suggests we should have a free trade area with Great Britain. I suggest to him that he could not do anything which would more quickly throw a great mass of workers in Canada out of jobs.
I want to take up one other thing which is particularly important to the Liberal party. They are the great traders, so-called. As I have said before, they traded us-they traded us down the river. For years and years and years they came out to western Canada and said on platforms there what a great thing free trade was for the farmers of western Canada. Then they came down here and spoke in favour of protection. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) has done the same thing even in the last few years. Out in the west he is a great free trader, saying: we have got to get rid of these tariffs. He did not say we must get rid of the subsidies, though it amounts to the same thing. But down here he said: we must increase the tariff on imported automobiles. This is the great Liberal line. I understand the hon.


member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh) criticized us severely because we did not increase tariffs enough to protect some of the industries in that area.
All we ask of industry in Canada is what the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been asking, namely that management and labour should get together with the designers to produce products which will show that Canada is not as stagnant as the Liberal party would like to make out, to show that we can produce these goods in Canada if we are given leadership by the government. I suggest we are getting that leadership now, and never before in our history has Canada had a trade minister with the vigour, the imagination and with the ability to go out and sell as we are honoured to have in Canada today. As I have said, we have listened over the years to the Liberal party and their bunch of nonsense. I am surprised that they should make any attempt to bring it up again.
Hon. members opposite like to talk about trade with Japan. We have, through negotiation and common ordinary horse trading, developed a better position in our trade with Japan than ever before in the history of this country. We sell to Japan grain and other basic raw materials that we never sold before. We are selling more than ever before; the gap between exports and imports has narrowed. We have done all these things and yet the opposition has the audacity to bring forward a grievance with regard to trade.
I turn now to a subject which is of particular interest to my home province, the question of oil and gas. We know the position of the Liberal party in this connection. They did not want to export any of it. They said: we have got to keep that at home. The hon. member for Laurier and the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat talked about a great free trade area including the inner six, the United States, Canada and perhaps the outer seven. Can hon. members see what would happen to our oil industry in Alberta if that were to come about? As a matter of fact, the only thing which has kept our oil industry progressive and kept jobs available in Alberta today in the oil industry has been the policy of this government with regard to oil and gas. There has been no other reason for it, and I want to compliment the Minister of Trade and Commerce for going out to Calgary not long ago and setting it on the line again to the international oil companies. I do not know if those companies paid the Liberal party before, but they certainly had them in their pockets when they wrecked the entire oil industry of Alberta. Talk about trade. These people do not know the meaning of the term. We should like to see this country, where it is at all feasible, use the

oil and gas produced in Alberta and Saskatchewan and in any other province that may have it. We commend the government for its oil policy and we commend the minister for having the courage to stand up and defend it and say it is going to be implemented if these international oil companies do not do what they should have done.
The question of gas is a similar one. How many people are working in Canada today because of the national energy board, because of the export of natural gas? We have these commodities which are in surplus in Canada, and hon. members opposite would have us join a free trade area controlled perhaps by their friends but certainly not controlled to the benefit of the people of Canada.
The hon. gentleman asks: what have you done? Well, we have increased our exports to the United Kingdom by somewhere in the neighbourhood of 16 per cent while our balance with the United States has remained relatively the same. In Ottawa itself we held a trade conference and put into operation a sales plan the like of which has never been seen here before under the leadership of a vigorous minister. I know the minister can be accused of all kinds of things in this regard. He can be accused of being theatrical. But for the first time in the history of this country we are doing something about trade. When gentlemen opposite say they know the meaning of the word, I say they do not.
As an example, only last year a retired farmer from Saskatchewan was instrumental in selling a million bushels of malting barley to Peru, a market that government officials had failed to contact. I have told the people of western Canada and suggested to the wheat pools out there, and in particular to the Saskatchewan wheat pool, which is rather vocal at times, in voicing some of its ideas, that if they spent half the money they spend campaigning against this government on getting out and selling some of the produce that they are handling in the markets of the world we should be a lot better off; and if the rest of the pools, the united grain growers and the other western organizations would show a greater concern about marketing their produce rather than depending on the government the export picture would look even better than it is. Here, of course, is where socialism falls down. Government people will never show the same enthusiasm for selling a product or take the same interest in doing this job. Again, if many people in private industry would take a lead from the Minister of Trade and Commerce and accept as their motto those initials which he has engraved on his cuff links we in western Canada in the farm areas would be a lot better off.

What else have we done? We have heard a lot of jeering and have been subjected to a lot of criticism with regard to the setting up of a productivity council. We have heard it is not going to be any good. We have heard you cannot take the best brains in the country and put them together and expect them to come up with anything. If we cannot control them, it is no good, our critics say. Perhaps this is the way they run their government but I am happy to be associated with a government which does not operate that way; a government with enough courage to take action with regard to setting up a productivity council to approach business, labour and representatives of agriculture and other forms of community endeavour in order to bring them together. We need something which will encourage us to lower our costs and which will help us to produce better so that we are more able to compete for world markets. We have been criticized for this by those people who think they know something about trade.
We have now on the order paper a bill sponsored by the Minister of Trade and Commerce in respect of a national design council. This is something of importance. We have a number of people in Canada today who are designing, inventing and producing new products who need leadership and help in getting these products into the right channels so that they can in turn help our over-all economic position. In spite of all these things the opposition maintain that we have done nothing.
I would also mention the baby budget, for which we have been criticized. I will have something more to say about the class or kind legislation but I want to say something in regard to my own constituency at this point.
The provisions of the baby budget in themselves have meant the difference between 400 men working, or not working, in my own constituency. These provisions made it possible for a pulp mill in my area to continue operating. In spite of that we have been told that we have done nothing.

speechtext: He has been out of order for the last half hour.

My hon. friend felt quite free to wander over the whole subject of trade and I therefore felt that I
3956	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Trade Policy should be permitted a reasonable time to tell him what we are doing and what we have done.
With regard to the dominion bureau of statistics' booklets put out a few months ago, I might say that they contain some of the most valuable information available to members of parliament and other Canadians who are interested. These two books are coloured blue and yellow and it is the blue book which is of particular interest to me because it indicates the products which are imported into Canada and particularly agricultural products. Canadian citizens in western Canada feel that our country is an agricultural country, and very properly so as this is the basic industry upon which we depend. However, if one looks at this book regarding agricultural products brought into this country, it will be seen that they amounted to approximately $681 million; $38 million from the United Kingdom and $365 million from the United States. In spite of this we are told that we have done nothing by the implementation of a national policy on agriculture, by diversifying the production on our farms and by setting up policies through which we can at least keep the domestic market for our own farmers. Are they free traders? No, they are not. If you attempted to explain the term "free trade", you would have difficulty in many parts of Canada.
Referring to this dominion bureau of statistics' book in regard to animal products imported, one finds that something in the neighbourhood of $143 million has been imported, $18 million from the United Kingdom and $82 million from the United States.
We are an agricultural country and we pride ourselves in this and base our economy on agriculture, yet these people have suggested that we join a free trade area. They have not referred to agriculture primarily because they do not know anything about it. I must mention that we do have problems regarding trade in respect of some of our agricultural products. We have a problem in western Canada regarding our sheep industry. We would like to see the importation of lambs and mutton from Australia and New Zealand confined to that period when our own lamb and mutton is not available to the market. We have made some progress in this regard and hope to make more so that our own farmers will have the advantage of the domestic market in this regard in Canada.
We have heard talk about free trade this afternoon. I suggest that this free trade is only a figment of Liberal imagination, and I use that word with a capital "L". They have spouted this policy during the years, particularly in western Canada, with the assistance


of a few particular newspapers which I think seriously gave their assistance for their own advantage and welfare rather than for the welfare of Canada as a whole. These hon. members suggest that we should have a free trade area with the United States. I would ask them how they propose to handle the wheat problem if they do have a free trade area. The United States has now a billion bushel surplus and at last count we had somewhere in the neighbourhood of between 500 and 700 million bushels surplus. Those hon. members suggest that they are going to solve this situation by having a free trade area. Perhaps they can solve the problem by giving the wheat away if they can find someone to take it. I would suggest somewhere along the line perhaps they will be willing to pay back to the farmers of western Canada the $600 million which they stole.
The things I have mentioned my hon. friends on the other side forget about when they start talking about trade. When the Prime Minister suggested we should try to divert 15 per cent of our trade from the United States to the United Kingdom he was speaking as a Canadian not representing western Canada but Canada as a whole. The hon. members for Laurier and Essex East spout at one moment for free traders but when they get back in their own ridings they then become high protection advocates. I am afraid that I am unable to follow that policy. I believe we must be good horse traders and am very proud that this government and particularly the Minister of Trade and Commerce, represent the best horse traders that I know.

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to rise and participate in this debate today because during the past year it has been my privilege to have attended several meetings of the standing committee of the NATO parliamentarians conference in Europe, during which time this question of trade was discussed at great length.
Today we are dealing with a motion made by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). I will read this motion in order to bring it back into perspective. It is as follows:
This house regrets the protectionist and inconsistent trade policies of the government and its failure to develop a long term foreign economic policy to enable Canada to participate fully in the challenging new opportunities in the field of international trade by implementing a vigorous program to promote the expansion of our secondary manufacturing industries and by encouraging the development of an Atlantic economic community.
I think perhaps it would be wise on my part to introduce at this point some background regarding this whole problem which has been raised by the opposition in the house

today. I am referring to the convention on the organization for economic co-operation and development which was recently passed by this House of Commons. I will just quote from article 1 which reads as follows:
The aims of the organization for economic co-operation and development (hereinafter called the "organization") shall be to promote policy-designed :
(a)	to achieve the highest sustainable economic growth and employment and a rising standard of living in member countries, while maintaining financial stability and thus to contribute to the development of the world economy;
(b)	to contribute to sound economic expansion in member as well as non-member countries in the process of economic development; and
(c)	to contribute to the expansion of world trade on a multilateral, non-discriminatory basis in accordance with international obligations.
I am sure that all hon. members are aware of the fact that this new organization for economic organization and development is the successor of a former organization which was known as the organization for European economic co-operation, the so-called O.E.E.C.
As you know, sir, a committee of four wise men was set up to study the whole question of O.E.E.C. and what future changes might be made in that organization. The
O.E.C.D. is the result of the study of the four wise men. The four wise men, of course, were Mr. Burgess, Mr. Clappier, Sir Paul Gore-Booth and Mr. Xenophon Zolotas. Ambassador Burgess of the United States was the chairman of this committee. They brought down their report in April, 1960. When one realizes that this report which was brought down by the four wise men was the precursor of this new organization whose convention we ratified, then there develops a kind of significance. I should like to quote from the report of the four wise men regarding matters of trade, and I shall attempt to correlate it with the amendment now before the house. I am quoting from page 27:
The aim of the O.E.E.C. was to restore the economy of its member countries and thus enable them to meet fully the trade and payments obligations arising from their undertakings in world organizations. Thus the O.E.E.C.'s first trade activities encouraged the development of trade primarily among its member countries, so as to complement the stimulus that American financial aid would be exerting on the European economy and reduce and even wipe out the dollar gap. Twelve years later, a high degree of success has been achieved in this direction-*
I might mention that the original O.E.E.C. was set up in April of 1948. I continue:
Twelve years later, a high degree of success has been achieved in this direction: balance of payments difficulties have, in general, disappeared; external convertibility of the principal currencies has been restored; and the liberalization of trade in industrial products is almost complete. Furthermore, the liberalization of trade in Europe has played an important role in unshackling world trade.

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy
But since the O.E.E.C.'s activity in the field of trade was in pursuit of objectives now largely achieved, and since it operated in a context which is now superseded, one might conclude that the future organization should do nothing in this field and abandon all the rules and procedures evolved in the course of 12 years of European co-operation.
One might be tempted to do this at first sight, since active co-operation in the field of trade, limited to the 18 European members of the O.E.E.C., runs up against the well-known objections which led governments to give us our task on January 14. Furthermore, bearing in mind the GATT rules and the duties (of various orders) which the industrialized countries recognize towards the underdeveloped countries, trade co-operation in a group consisting of the United States, Canada and the 18 members of the O.E.E.C. would evoke similar objections.
Nevertheless, since commercial policy, as an element in general economic policy, will certainly be within the responsibility of the future organization, it is difficult to imagine that such a clear-cut answer would be acceptable. Nor, moreover, would it be opportune, since the initial objectives of the
O.E.E.C. have not been fully achieved by all its members. On the other hand it should be publicly accepted that the trade activity of the future organization will be carried on according to the principles of the GATT.
In making reference to these remarks of the four wise men, I am going to point out something which apparently has not been too apparent in this house. The people who are today proposing a free trade area of the Atlantic economic community; that is to say, of the free western world as we know it, are the people who in the year 1948 did not see fit even to join as full members the organization which at that time was known as the
O.E.E.C. At that time Canada and the United States were only associate members of this organization which in the years which followed developed such great success in the field of trade and in the recovery which took place in Europe. Today we are being asked to create a free trade area. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce who replied to the amendment today made it very clear that this was a switch in the thinking of members of the opposition.
The hon. member who spoke just prior to me made it very clear that there are men who speak for the opposition in this parliament who one day say one thing and another day say another thing because when this opportunity was presented to them when they were members of the government they rejected it; they did not become members of this great Atlantic community when they had an opportunity to do so. But they criticize the present government for not doing enough, although Canada has now become a full member of the organization for economic co-operation and development.
There is an impression about that by being part of an organization such as the Atlantic economic community, then suddenly all barriers will disappear and we shall have what

Alleged Lack of Trade Policy I might describe as an almost idealistic state of no tariff barriers whatsoever. I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that this is not so even today in the common market among the so-called inner six of Europe who are close to economic integration and, yes, I might even suggest there is some tendency toward political integration in this particular grouping; they have not eliminated all their tariff barriers. In fact, they are progressively taking action to bring about certain changes. On July 1, 1960, the first set of internal tariff reductions in the E.E.C., which is the inner six, and the first set of these for the E.F.T.A., which is the outer seven in Europe, came into operation. In each organization their internal customs duties were lowered by 20 per cent on the basic duty. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, sometimes when we listen to the debates in this house and we hear about these free trade offers we feel that there will be no tariffs, and all this criticism about protectionists and inconsistent trade policies of the government simply flows out of the window because it just does not make sense. For example, the Federal Republic of Germany, which is a member of the inner six, also has a lot of its trade outside of the grouping known as the inner six. I might say that a high proportion of its trade is with what we call the outer seven and it has lower tariffs than the others. Tariff reduction has been used on their part to curtail inflation in that country. Germany, which is a member of the inner six, is obliged to raise its tariffs from July 1, 1960, and again before December 1, 1960, in accordance with the proposals of the commission of the European community. Therefore, we see that this proposal for a free trade area is not as simple a proposition as it is being made out by the speakers who have spoken for the opposition.
We might refer to some of the problems which face the inner six and the outer seven in Europe. Perhaps we should not forget that in that so-called Atlantic community which we speak loosely of as the inner six and the outer seven there are other, as it were, forgotten countries of the western world such as Greece, Turkey, Spain, Ireland, Finland and Iceland.
Finland has joined the free trade association.

Yes, but not in a direct way. My hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillin-gate interrupts.
There have also been contacts with other countries in Europe but not as part of the structure as we understand it and as we know it. These changes have taken place in Europe. These blocs have been formed, the inner six and the outer seven and we find there are

great difficulties in achieving further integration of the inner six and the outer seven.
Reference might be made here to the position of the United Kingdom in this regard. At the present time the United Kingdom does not adhere to the treaty of Rome for several reasons, two of which I think are of great importance. The first is, of course, the United Kingdom's connection with the commonwealth. Some people suggest that this is not a very important force but when one realizes the extent of the trade of the United Kingdom it then becomes another matter.
The commonwealth is the world's largest preferential trading organization. Sometimes some of the hon. members to my right do not seem to be aware of that. Its exports are about 19,000 million annually or over 25 per cent of total world exports excluding trade between members of the Soviet bloc. Its imports are more than 110 million and represent 30 per cent of world imports. One-quarter of the world's population lives in the commonwealth.
A high proportion of commonwealth trade Is in primary commodities from underdeveloped countries, some of whom are wholly dependent upon the United Kingdom market. It is politically unthinkable for the United Kingdom to enter into any agreement with the Six which would have as its effect the ruin of even a small British colony or country. Such action would be the end of whatever influence the United Kingdom possesses as the motherland of the commonwealth.
These things are very significant, Mr. Speaker. The fact is that there are these great divisions among the nations of Europe and they have not been able to find common ground in the European field even though they were members of the organization for European co-operation for so many years. Even with the efforts of the organization for European economic co-operation, its success can be measured by the fact that two distinct trading blocs have developed.
From what I have observed in Europe I may say that despite all the efforts which have been made on both sides there does not seem to be thus far a coming together of the thinking of the leaders of the two blocs. There is no question that the inner bloc is a much more strongly integrated organization than the E.F.T.A. which is a rather loosely organized group. Nevertheless, there are the difficulties that arise primarily because of the position of the United Kingdom which out of deference to other members of the commonwealth will not sacrifice the preferential treatment it accords to them and vice versa.
The problem has been tackled by many of the leading lights of Europe in the field

of economics but no conclusions have been reached yet. The commission of the European economic community is an organization headed by Professor Hallstein, a very distinguished European in the field of trade, and on March 28, 1960 he said in Strasbourg that it will be possible for the community- the inner six-to show good will toward all other GATT members by reducing the level of the common external tariff. He went on to say that such a move, if it were matched by reciprocal action, would "open the way, particularly in Europe, to tariff reductions which will take into account all the essential needs of European trade".
We hear talk about tariffs being wiped out lock, stock and barrel but this is not so. In the few minutes I have been speaking I think I have been able to demonstrate that even within that group which we know as the inner six there are tariff barriers which are applied on the part of those countries belonging to the inner six with respect to the members of the outer seven. In the case of some members of the inner six these tariffs are more lenient than in the case of others. In particular, I refer to the'German system of tariffs which provides for lower tariffs so far as members of the outer seven are concerned than is the case with some of the other countries belonging to the inner six.
Members of the opposition have brought up the question of free trade in the Atlantic economic community. I think there is no question that when the minister replied to the charges of the opposition he made it very clear that on this continent we might suffer greatly if the type of program being put forward by those who sit on my right were implemented because we have problems of which Canadians are well aware. There is the problem of transportation. The hon. member who preceded me spoke about the problem of the cost of transporting various items from eastern Canada to western Canada. What would their suggestion mean to our economy? What would it mean to Canada's economy in general? I would think that the hon. member who moved the amendment and
Business of the House
his supporters are suggesting something in which they themselves do not believe because, as I have gone to some trouble to point out, when they had the opportunity in 1948 to become a part of this Atlantic community- and we all admit it has had certain successful results-they rejected the idea. Yet they come into the house today and say that the present government, which was the first government to ratify the new O.E.C.D. convention, is not doing the thing which they themselves failed to do when they had the opportunity to do so in 1948 and which, if they had had the foresight to do so, would have meant that we would not have the problems in the field of trade that we face in Canada today.
We have a minister who works hard, who is selling as much as he can, who is promoting trade for Canada, and I am sure the people of Canada are grateful that such a minister is occupying this position today. The point I should like to make is that those who have introduced the amendment had an opportunity to do something in this field. They had a chance to become a full member of the Atlantic economic community and they rejected it. May I call it ten o'clock?
